addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)
- dev: TDD Developer agent - implements features using test-driven development and clean code principles (Tools: All tools)

- entire-search: Search Entire checkpoint history and transcripts with `entire search --json`. Use proactively when the user asks about previous work, commits, sessions, prompts, or historical context in this repository. (Tools: Bash)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- reviewer: Code review agent - critically reviews changes for quality, security, and correctness (Tools: All tools)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

- test-doc: Use this agent when the user needs markdown files created in the test-files/ directory. This includes generating test data files, sample documentation, mock content, or any markdown-formatted files for testing purposes.

Examples:

<example>
Context: User needs sample markdown files for testing a documentation parser.
user: "I need some sample markdown files to test my parser"
assistant: "I'll use the markdown-file-generator agent to create sample markdown files in the test-files/ directory for your parser testing."
<Task tool invocation to launch markdown-file-generator agent>
</example>

<example>
Context: User is setting up test fixtures and needs markdown content.
user: "Create a few test markdown files with different heading levels and formatting"
assistant: "Let me use the markdown-file-generator agent to create markdown files with varied formatting in the test-files/ directory."
<Task tool invocation to launch markdown-file-generator agent>
</example>

<example>
Context: User needs mock README files for testing.
user: "Generate some fake README files for my test suite"
assistant: "I'll invoke the markdown-file-generator agent to create mock README files in the test-files/ directory."
<Task tool invocation to launch markdown-file-generator agent>
</example> (Tools: All tools)

attachment.content:
- agent-integration: Run all three agent integration phases sequentially: research, write-tests, and implement using E2E-first TDD (unit tests written last). For individual phases, use /agent-integration:research, /agent-integration:write-tests, or /agent-integration:implement. Use when the user says "integrate agent", "add agent support", or wants to run the full agent integration pipeline end-to-end.
- changelog: Generate or update the CHANGELOG.md for a new release version. Use when the user says "generate changelog", "update changelog", "write release notes", or asks to prepare a changelog for a version like "changelog for 0.5.3".
- e2e: Orchestrate E2E test triage and fix implementation: runs triage-ci then implement sequentially. Accepts test names, --agent, artifact path, or CI run reference. For individual phases, use /e2e:triage-ci, /e2e:debug, or /e2e:implement. Use when the user says "triage e2e", "fix e2e failures", or wants the full triage-to-fix pipeline.
- entire: How to use the Entire CLI (checkpoints, search, sessions, and more). Use whenever a task involves entire, checkpoints, or the `entire` command.
- test-repo: Use this skill to test strategy changes against a fresh test repository. Invoke when the user asks to "test against a test repo", "validate the changes", or wants to verify session hooks, commits, and rewind functionality work correctly.
- analyst: Requirements analyst agent - gathers, clarifies, and documents requirements
- dev: TDD Developer agent - implements features using test-driven development and clean code principles
- dev-cycle: Orchestrates the development cycle - developer implements, reviewer critiques, repeat until done
- reviewer: Code review agent - critically reviews changes for quality, security, and correctness
- e2e:debug: Deep-dive artifact analysis for diagnosing E2E test failures
- e2e:implement: Apply fixes from triage/debug findings, verify with scoped E2E tests
- e2e:triage-ci: Triage E2E failures via local reruns or CI artifacts, classify flaky vs real-bug, present findings report
- agent-integration:implement: E2E-first Test driven development — unit tests written last
- agent-integration:research: Assess a new agent's hook/lifecycle compatibility with the Entire CLI
- agent-integration:write-tests: Create E2E agent runner (no unit tests)
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

content.content:
Find the code for a task from a plain-language query (start here)

Usage:
  entire graph search --query "issue or concept" --repo . [--top-k 10] [--format text|json|ndjson|agent] [--head] [--profile fast|full] [--deep]

Ranked source regions for a plain-language description, with source and file:line inline, budgeted to drop straight into context. This is the first move for almost every locate task.

By default search returns: ranked candidate fix sites (top hits as full function bodies), RELATED SITES, the COVERING TEST plus other tests over the same code (ALSO COVERING), SAME-CONCEPT LITERAL (every place the concept is named, tagged EDIT/CONSUMER/DOC), a VERIFY line (the narrowest test command for the file), and a CLOSED-SET WARNING when a switch over a sealed set would fail at runtime. The three reference blocks (container map, signature types, declaration card) are OFF by default because they cost turns in agent sessions; --reference-blocks all turns them on for interactive reading.

--top-k only changes how many results come back; --deep additionally runs the exhaustive sparse (BM25) pass and fuses it with the semantic ranking (slower, reads every eligible file).

Flags:
  --query <text>            The task or bug in one plain sentence (required)
  --repo <path>             Repository to search (default: current repo)
  --top-k <n>               Number of results to return (default: 10)
  --format text|json|ndjson|agent
                            Output format; text is tiered for reading, agent is compact (default: json)
  --head                    Search the committed tree (cached) instead of the working tree
  --profile syntax-only|fast|full
                            Parsing depth; use full for bug-fix/locate (call-graph active) (default: fast)
  --deep                    Also run the exhaustive BM25 pass and fuse it (slower)
  --max-context-bytes <n>   Output byte budget; 0 = unbounded (default: 24576)
  --reference-blocks all|container-map,signature-types,type-card
                            Turn reference blocks back on (off by default)
  --max-indexed-files <n>   Bound cold-search parsing to N files
  --index-all-files         Widen cold-search parsing to every file
  --cache-dir <path>        Override the committed-tree cache directory
  --no-cache                Disable the committed-tree cache

Examples:
  entire graph search --repo . --query "token refresh returns 401" --format text --top-k 8
  entire graph search --repo . --query "csv export ordering" --profile full

content.content:
#!/bin/sh
# Entire CLI local-development hook launcher.
#
# In local-dev mode, Entire hooks invoke the CLI straight from source via
# "go run", which recompiles on demand. When the tree does not compile (for
# example while an agent is resolving a merge conflict) "go run" fails and the
# hook would silently do nothing. This launcher first checks that the tree
# builds; if it does it runs the freshly compiled CLI, otherwise it falls back
# to an "entire" binary on PATH. If neither is available it exits 0 so it never
# blocks the surrounding git or agent operation.
#
# Usage: scripts/entire-dev <entire args...>
#
# All local-dev hooks delegate here so the build-probe-and-fallback logic lives
# in one place rather than being duplicated across generated hook commands.

set -eu

# Informational messages go to stderr so they never pollute hook stdout (some
# hooks emit JSON there).
log() {
	printf '[entire-dev] %s\n' "$1" >&2
}

# Resolve the repository root from this script's own location so it works
# regardless of the caller's working directory. Parameter expansion avoids
# depending on external tools like dirname, which may not be on PATH when this
# runs from a minimal hook environment.
case "$0" in
	*/*) script_dir=${0%/*} ;;

- `.claude/skills/entire/SKILL.md` (agent-help pointer, v1 managed), plus `agent-integration`, `changelog`, `e2e`, `test-repo`.
- `entire-search` subagent registered for Claude Code, Gemini, and Codex; `entire.md`/`entire.toml` skill mirrors for Gemini and Codex.

- `entire graph doctor`: plugin data dir writable, no-egress mode on.
- The durable index was missing, so every query was rebuilding from scratch. I built it: **1,226 files, 24,630 symbols, 135,926 relations, completeness `ok`** (Go, plus Bash/JSON/Markdown/TS/YAML/TOML). Cache now lives in `~/.local/share/entire/plugins/data/graph/search` (15 MB).

Two things worth your attention:

**1. Search latency is high on this repo.** Worktree search ~19s, `--head` (cached committed tree) ~43s. The cached path is *slower* because it ranks over all 24.6k symbols while the worktree path preselects down to ~8.4k. That's backwards from what `--head` implies, and 19-43s per locate call is enough that agents will quietly go back to grepping. Might be worth a look as a product issue, not just a local config one.

**2. Your brew CLI is 0.9.0; 0.10.6 is out.** I did not upgrade it. You have an active tracked session right now and the hooks run through `scripts/entire-dev` (source build) anyway, so the brew binary is only the fallback. Upgrading mid-session is the one thing here that could plausibly break hook behavior. Say the word and I'll run `brew upgrade --yes entire`.

There's the other flow too, which also opens a browser pings a loopback listener when successfully authenticated, which is smoother. What would it take to use that as default, and put the current flow behind a `--device` flag? detailed plan please. the backend already supports it.

That prompt is why `runLogin` has the shape it has now: loopback-browser default, device flow demoted to a fallback.

## Model timeline for `login.go`

Opus 4.6 (Mar) → Opus 4.7 (May) → Opus 4.8 (Jun 2-4) → Fable 5 (Jun 10 onward). 40 commits, ~30 with model attribution. Four commits have no model at all: Sven Pfleiderer's two Mar-31 review fixes, Rizel Scarlett's May-01 clipboard change, and `goose-guest`'s May-14 follow-up.

## Three caveats

**1. I picked the function.** "The authentication function" is ambiguous here — there's also `PostOAuthToken` (`internal/entireclient/httputil/oauth.go:91`), `LoginTokenForContext` (`auth/contexts.go:209`), and `ResolveControlPlaneTarget` (`auth/control_plane.go:47`). **2. Model came from the commit trailer, not the checkpoint.** The session index returned `model: null` for the June session; I read `Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context)` off the `Co-Authored-By` line. For the March sessions the index did carry `claude-opus-4-6[1m]` directly. Worth knowing that those two sources disagree in coverage.

**3. Most pre-July checkpoints aren't locally resolvable.** This clone uses the ref-based backend (`refs/entire/checkpoints/XX/<ULID>`), but commits from March-June carry short-ID trailers from the old v1-branch backend. `entire checkpoint explain 334df9885` fails with *"checkpoint not found: 224fb4e17934"*, and `refs/heads/entire/checkpoints/v1` doesn't exist on origin. I recovered the June prompt through the server-side `entire search`, which indexes all 6,731 checkpoints and does have it. So the data is intact — the local resolution path just can't reach the older format. That's a real papercut if you expect `explain` to work on any historical commit.

content.text:
## What actually broke

It's not a semantic misread. It's a lexical one, and I can show you the exact line.

Single-term probes against this repo:

| Query | Top score | Top hit |
|---|---|---|
| `auth` | **34.6** | `addInsecureHTTPAuthFlag` ✓ |
| `login` | **31.0** | `persistLogin` ✓ |
| `logs` | **31.1** | `RestoreLogsOnly` |
| `authentication` | **16.6** | `addInsecureHTTPAuthFlag`, then `slugifyTitle`, `HTTPErrorMessage` ✗ |

`authentication` scores **half** what `auth` scores on the same target. So in the combined query, `logs` (31) simply outbid `authentication` (16.6) and dragged the whole ranking into the logging package. Nothing about "user login" was ever weighed.

The culprit is `internal/sem/search.go:2837`:

```go
func searchNameContainsTerm(lowerName, term string) bool {
	if len(term) < 3 { return false }
	if strings.Contains(lowerName, term) { return true }
	// ... strips trailing "es", then trailing "s"
	return false
}
```

Substring match plus plural stripping. That's the entire morphology. `strings.Contains("runlogin", "authentication")` is false, so `runLogin` scores **zero** name coverage on the most meaningful word in the query. Meanwhile `"restorelogsonly"` contains `"logs"` and scores a full hit.

There's a second, subtler failure in the same line: because it's substring and not token-aware, `log` matches `runLogin` *and* `RestoreLogsOnly` equally. The one signal that could separate login from logging is actively conflating them.

## Three defects, in order of payoff

**1. No abbreviation expansion. This is the whole bug.** Code is written in abbreviations and prose is not. `authentication→auth` is the same class as `configuration→config`, `database→db`, `repository→repo`, `initialize→init`, `context→ctx`, `request→req`, `implementation→impl`, `transaction→txn`. Every one of those will fail identically today. The graph is plural-tolerant but not abbreviation-tolerant, which is backwards for identifiers: developers pluralize rarely and abbreviate constantly.

Fix: a static bidirectional alias table consulted inside `searchNameContainsTerm`. Match-time only, so no reindex and no migration. ~40 entries covers most of it.

**2. Name coverage is deliberately not IDF-weighted, and that overcorrected.** The comment above `searchNameTermCoverage` (line 2814) makes a real argument, calibrated on hugo#12171: rare prose words like "similarly" and "adjacent" appear in no identifier, so IDF weighting pushed the denominator onto unmatchable words. Correct diagnosis. But dropping rarity weighting entirely also removed the defense against *ubiquitous* code words. In a Go repo where every file imports a logging package, `log` is worth approximately nothing, and right now it counts exactly as much as a rare domain noun.

Don't restore full IDF, that would re-break hugo. Add a **document-frequency ceiling**: if a term appears in more than some share of indexed symbol names, its name-coverage contribution drops to zero. That nulls `log`, `get`, `new`, `run`, `handle`, `client`, `error` while leaving mid-frequency domain nouns like `pages` and `section` fully weighted. Hugo's fix survives; this failure doesn't.

Pair it with **token-boundary matching** — split identifiers on camelCase/snake_case and compare whole tokens. Then `log` matches token `logs`, but not token `login`, and the two concepts stop colliding.

**3. The LOW CONFIDENCE message told you something false.** It printed:

> `top score 22.3 (weak, below 12)`

22.3 is not below 12. Looking at `AssessSearchConfidence` (`search_confidence.go:159`), the score ladder passed cleanly — `Low` was set by the *tie* test at line 197 (ranks 1 and 2 were 0.01 apart). The renderer at `internal/cli/search.go:1303` then unconditionally formats the "weak, below N" clause regardless of which test fired. The code's own comment at line 185 says these mechanical tests exist precisely to catch "a payload that scores WELL" — the message contradicts the design. One-line fix: branch the wording on `assessment.Reason`.

Worth noting the tie test *did* fire correctly here, and the ranking *was* a coin flip. The warning was right and the explanation was wrong, which is arguably worse than no warning.

## What I'd ship

Defect 1 first, alone. It's the highest-leverage change, it's a lookup table, and it needs no reindex. Defect 3 is a one-liner, ship it alongside. Defect 2 is the interesting one but it's a ranking change with a real regression surface, so it wants the bench harness behind it.

Which you have: `bench/`, `cmd/graph-bench`, `internal/bench`, plus explicit guard tests on the hugo case at `internal/sem/search_test.go:2206-2221`. So this is measurable rather than vibes.

One thing worth deciding before any of it: a cheap complementary win is **compound joining at query time** — `logs in → login`, `sign in → signin`, `roll back → rollback`, `check out → checkout`, `clean up → cleanup`, `fall back → fallback`. Your own codebase contains every one of those as a single identifier, and natural prose splits every one of them. That would have fixed *this specific query* without touching the ranker at all. It's narrower than abbreviation expansion but nearly free.

Want me to write the alias table plus the confidence-message fix and run it against the bench?

# AGENTS.md — operating guide for coding agents

Hand this to any coding agent working in a repo where the `entire graph` plugin
is installed. It moves initial code-location work from broad grep/read
exploration to targeted graph queries; token impact depends on the task and
model, and no end-to-end savings claim is current.

## What this gives you

A precomputed, **deterministic** code graph is available through the `entire graph` command — functions, classes, methods, types, routes, and the calls/inheritance/field/service relations between them, parsed with tree-sitter, 100% locally (no network, no model, no keys). Use it to **LOCATE** and **UNDERSTAND** code *before* broad grep / find / cat / whole-file exploration. Every command is no-egress and safe to run inside a sandboxed session. The same commit yields the same graph, but static relations can be heuristic or incomplete; inspect focused source and verify the resulting change.

Default flags to remember: pass `--repo .` when you're not inside an Entire session; the graph reads your **working tree by default** (your uncommitted edits are visible), and `--head` switches to committed-tree semantics with a cached, reusable index.

---

## The parts of the graph

Reach for the smallest tool that answers your question.

### 🔍 search — *find the code for a task* (your first move)
Ranked source regions for a plain-language description, with the source and `file:line` inline. Hybrid ranking over bodies, identifiers (camelCase/snake_case aware), signatures, paths, and graph neighbors. Output is budgeted (16 KiB by default) to drop straight into context.

```sh
entire graph search --repo . --query "<the task or bug in one plain sentence>" --format text --top-k 8
```

- `--format agent` for compact ranked output with latency telemetry; `json`/`ndjson` for the full schema (completeness, partial failures, diagnostics).
- `--top-k N` result count; `--max-context-bytes N` byte budget (`0` = unbounded).
- Working tree by default; add `--head` for committed-tree + cache reuse.
- `--profile syntax-only|fast|full` (default `fast`); `--index-all-files` or `--max-indexed-files N` to widen/bound cold-search parsing.

**When:** the start of essentially every task. One good query lands you on the fix area.

### 🕸️ neighbors — *who calls this / what does it call* (targeted relations)
Direct incoming/outgoing relations for **one** symbol, with definition locations, plus bounded two-hop paths at `--depth 2`. For the full blast radius of a change, prefer `impact`; use `neighbors` when you want one specific relation/direction. Never `edges` for this (full stream).

```sh
entire graph neighbors --repo . --symbol NAME --relation CALLS --direction in   # who calls NAME
entire graph neighbors --repo . --symbol NAME --relation CALLS --direction out  # what NAME calls
```

content.content:
# Semantic Provider Benchmark

`graph-bench` clones popular real-world repositories per language and measures the
semantic provider over them, emitting a machine-readable performance and quality
report. It originated as the WP10 harness in the
[archived v2 implementation plan](../docs/archive/2026-06-18-entire-graph-v2-implementation-plan.md)
and is meant to be re-run each work phase to track regressions and quality gains.

## Design

- **Clone phase (network) is separate from measurement (no-egress).** Cloning
  uses `git`; the measured analysis runs `BuildProviderSnapshot` with
  `NoNetwork` set, so the path we benchmark is the same local-only path the
  provider guarantees in production.
- **Cloned repos never enter our commits.** They live under `bench/.cache/`,
  which is gitignored.
- **Repeatable.** `bench/repos.json` lists the repositories; `bench/repos.lock.json`
  pins each to an exact commit. Commit the lock file so every phase analyzes the
  same source and the numbers are comparable.

## Tiers

| Tier | Manifest               | Repos               | When                                          |
| ---- | ---------------------- | ------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| Fast | `bench/repos.fast.json`| 3/language (72)     | Routine per-phase tracking; runs in minutes.  |
| Full | `bench/repos.json`     | 10/language (240)   | Occasional deep runs; includes mega-repos.    |

The fast tier is a curated subset of the full manifest (no mega-repos like
linux/tensorflow/vscode), so its repos share the same `repos.lock.json` pins and
clone cache — no separate lock needed. The full tier is comprehensive but gated
by a handful of giant repositories and can take 1.5-3 hours.

## Layout

| Path                     | Purpose                                                |
| ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| `bench/repos.json`       | Full manifest: 10 popular repos per language.          |
| `bench/repos.fast.json`  | Fast manifest: 3 repos per language (subset of full).  |
| `bench/repos.lock.json`  | Commit pins for reproducibility (covers both tiers).   |
| `bench/.cache/`          | Cloned repositories (gitignored).                      |

entire graph search --repo . --profile full \
  --query "the main authentication function that logs a user in"
```

Top hits, measured against `entireio/cli`:

| Rank | Score | Symbol |
| ---- | ----- | ------ |
| 1 | 22.3 | `ManualCommitStrategy.RestoreLogsOnly` |
| 2 | 22.3 | `handleLogsOnlyRewindNonInteractive` |
| 3 | 20.5 | `newDoctorLogsCmd` |
| 4 | 20.1 | `restoreResumeSessions` |

Nothing in the head is authentication. `runLogin`, `persistLogin` and the whole `auth` package are absent.

## Why

Single-term probes isolate it:

| Query | Top score | Head quality |
| ----- | --------- | ------------ |
| `auth` | **34.6** | clean — `addInsecureHTTPAuthFlag`, `runAuthenticatedDataAPI`, `NewAuthenticatedAPIClient` |
| `login` | **31.0** | clean — `persistLogin`, `RecordLoginContext`, `NewRefreshingLoginProvider` |
| `logs` | **31.1** | logging |
| `authentication` | **16.6** | noise — `slugifyTitle`, `HTTPErrorMessage`, `newRepoVisibilityCmd` |

`authentication` scores **half** what `auth` scores on the same concept, so in the combined sentence `logs` (31) simply outbids it and drags the ranking into logging. The prose spelling of the most meaningful word in the query contributes almost nothing.

## Defect 1 — no abbreviation expansion (fix proposed)

`searchNameContainsTerm` (`internal/sem/search.go`) is a substring test with plural tolerance and nothing else:

```go
if strings.Contains(lowerName, term) { return true }
// ... strips trailing "es", then trailing "s"
```

`strings.Contains("runlogin", "authentication")` is false, so every correct answer scores **zero** name coverage on the query's key term, while `"restorelogsonly"` contains `"logs"` and scores a full hit.

This is not specific to auth. Code is written in abbreviations and prose is not, so the same failure is waiting for `configuration`/`config`, `database`/`db`, `repository`/`repo`, `initialize`/`init`, `context`/`ctx`, `request`/`req`, `implementation`/`impl`, `transaction`/`txn`. The matcher is plural-tolerant but not abbreviation-tolerant, which is backwards for identifiers: developers pluralize rarely and abbreviate constantly.

**Proposed fix** (branch `fix/search-abbreviation-expansion`): a long-to-short alias table consulted when the literal spelling misses. Match-time only, so no reindex and no format change.

Matching is **token-scoped**, not substring, because abbreviations are short enough to manufacture hits (`int` for `integer` would match `interface`, `internal`, `print`). Two thresholds by length:

- **4+ chars** match a token **prefix or suffix** — carries `auth` → `Authenticated`, `config` → `Configured`, and at the suffix end `repo` → `gitrepo`, `auth` → `oauth`. Anchoring both ends rather than allowing a free substring keeps `spec` → `inspect` out, since `inspect` ends in `spect`.
- **2–3 chars** must match a **whole token** — stops `req` → `frequency` and `db` → `debug`, while still catching the standalone `ctx`, `req`, `err`, `db` that code writes as its own token.

### Measured effect

| Query | Before | After |
| ----- | ------ | ----- |
| `authentication` | 16.6, noisy head | **19.9**, head is `addInsecureHTTPAuthFlag`, `LooksLikeSSHAuthFailure`, `newAuthStatusCmd` |
| the full sentence | logging at 1–5, no auth in top 5 | **unchanged at 1–5**; auth enters at ranks 6, 11, 12 |

**This does not fix the headline query, and the issue should stay open until Defect 2 is done.** Name coverage contributes `10 × matched/3`, and both `addInsecureHTTPAuthFlag` and `RestoreLogsOnly` carry exactly one of this query's terms, so at the coverage layer they **tie**. The table removes the auth side's zero; it does not outrank logging. The remaining gap is BM25 body score, which Defect 2 addresses.

Full `./internal/...` suite passes, including the hugo#12171 guard.

## Defect 2 — name coverage is substring-based and frequency-blind (open)

Two compounding problems in the same signal.

**2a. Substring matching conflates `login` with `logging`.** Because the test runs over the lowercased name, `logs` → `log` → `strings.Contains("runlogin", "log")` is **true**. The one signal that could separate login from logging matches both identically. Splitting identifiers into camelCase/snake tokens and comparing whole tokens would let `login` match `runLogin`'s token exactly while `logs` → `log` would not.

**2b. `searchNameTermCoverage` is deliberately not IDF-weighted.** The comment above it makes a real argument calibrated on gohugoio/hugo#12171: rare prose words like "similarly" and "adjacent" appear in no identifier, so IDF weighting pushed the denominator onto unmatchable words. Correct diagnosis — but dropping rarity weighting entirely also removed the defense against *ubiquitous* code words. In a Go repo where every file imports a logging package, `log` is worth approximately nothing, yet it counts exactly as much as a rare domain noun.

Suggested shape: don't restore full IDF (that re-breaks hugo). Add a **document-frequency ceiling** — if a term appears in more than some share of indexed symbol names, its name-coverage contribution drops to zero. That nulls `log`, `get`, `new`, `run`, `handle`, `client`, `error` while leaving mid-frequency domain nouns like `pages` and `section` fully weighted.

`internal/sem/search_test.go` now pins the 2a behaviour so fixing it surfaces as a deliberate assertion change rather than silent drift.

## Also worth doing — compound joining at query time

Prose splits compounds that code writes as one identifier: `logs in` → `login`, `sign in` → `signin`, `roll back` → `rollback`, `check out` → `checkout`, `clean up` → `cleanup`, `fall back` → `fallback`. `entireio/cli` contains every one of those as a single identifier. Narrower than Defect 1 but nearly free, and it would have fixed this specific query on its own.

## Gap — no offline retrieval eval

Ranking quality is currently guarded by hand-measured cases embedded in unit tests and code comments. `bench/` is a performance and coverage harness over 72–240 cloned repos, not a gold-site retrieval eval, and it needs network. There is no way to ask "did this ranking change help or hurt across a corpus" without doing it by hand, which is why Defect 2 is riskier to land than Defect 1. Worth its own issue.

## Not a defect — already fixed

An earlier read of a stale checkout flagged the `LOW CONFIDENCE` notice for printing `top score 22.3 (weak, below 12)` when 22.3 is not below 12. That is **already fixed** on `main` (`internal/cli/search.go`), which now gates the "below" suffix on the score as displayed. Recording it so nobody re-reports it.

## Next steps

- [x] Defect 1 — abbreviation table, token-scoped matching, tests
- [ ] Defect 2a — token-boundary matching for name coverage
- [ ] Defect 2b — document-frequency ceiling on name-coverage terms
- [ ] Compound joining at query time
- [ ] Offline retrieval eval so ranking changes are measurable

Defect 3 done and committed. **`41e0a45e`** on `fix/search-compound-joining`, branched off `main`, +226 lines, not pushed.

## It works

| Query | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| "...that logs a user in" | 22.3, logging cluster, no auth in top 5 | **28.0**, all auth/login |
| "the user cannot log in" | — | 37.2 `newLoginCmd`, `RecordLoginContext` |
| "write the log in json format" | — | JSON/log code, no auth |

## Two things the measurement caught that I'd have shipped wrong

**Phrasal verbs are separable.** My first implementation scanned adjacent word pairs and changed *nothing* on the exact query that motivated it. The sentence is "logs **a user** in" — verb and particle four tokens apart. My whole premise in the issue ("`logs in` → `login`") was based on a bigram that never appears in the query. Now it looks ahead up to three tokens for a particle, gated on the next token opening an object phrase.

**The adjacent case needed a part-of-speech cue, and my "bounded cost" claim was false.** "cannot log in" is a phrasal verb; "write the log in json format" is noun + preposition. English spells them identically. I pinned that as a documented limitation on the grounds that the joined term is only *added*, so the damage is small. Then I measured it: `persistLogin`, `RecordLoginContext` and `runLogin` took ranks 1, 2 and 3 of that logging query. It hijacked it completely. A determiner immediately before the head now marks it as a noun and blocks the join; noun compounds like "the end point" are exempt since a determiner there is expected.

That's twice now I asserted a mechanism and the measurement contradicted it — the DF ceiling, then this. The pattern is consistent enough that I'd treat any unmeasured claim in #247 as suspect.

One clean property worth having: queries containing no compound are **provably** unaffected, since nothing enters the term set unless the table fires. No regression surface outside compound queries.

Defect 3 is implemented and committed (`41e0a45e` on `fix/search-compound-joining`, branched off `main`, not pushed). It fixes the headline query. Two findings along the way, both of which correct things this issue previously asserted.

## Result

| Query | Before | After |
| ----- | ------ | ----- |
| `the main authentication function that logs a user in` | 22.3, logging cluster, no auth in top 5 | **28.0** — `fetchCurrentUserLogin`, `parseLoginServer`, `RecordLoginContext`, `NewRefreshingLoginProvider` |
| `the user cannot log in` | — | 37.2 — `newLoginCmd`, `RecordLoginContext` |
| `write the log in json format` | — | JSON/log code only, no auth pollution |

Queries containing no compound are *provably* unaffected: nothing enters the term set unless the table fires. The regression surface is limited to compound-bearing queries.

## Finding 1 — phrasal verbs are separable, and this issue's premise was a bigram that never occurs

This issue said the fix was `logs in` → `login`. That bigram **does not appear in the motivating query**. The sentence is "the authentication function that logs **a user** in" — verb and particle four tokens apart, split around the object, which is what English does with separable phrasal verbs.

The first implementation scanned adjacent pairs, exactly as this issue described, and changed **nothing** on the query that motivated it. The scan now looks ahead up to three tokens for a particle, gated on the following token opening an object phrase (`a`, `the`, `its`, `them`, …). Noun compounds (`end point`, `meta data`) are not separable and stay adjacent-only.

## Finding 2 — adjacent joins need a part-of-speech cue; "the cost is bounded" was wrong

`cannot log in` is a phrasal verb. `write the log in json format` is noun + preposition. English spells them identically.

An earlier draft of this change pinned that collision as an accepted limitation, reasoning that the joined term is only *added*, never substituted, so the cost is small. Measured, it is not:

```
query: "write the log in json format"
  1  34.8  persistLogin
  2  34.0  RecordLoginContext
  3  34.2  runLogin
  6  30.2  promoteNextLogin
```

A legitimate logging query hijacked outright at ranks 1-3. An added term that matches a dense cluster of real identifiers wins regardless of being additive.

Fix: a determiner immediately before the head (`the log in`) marks it as a noun and disqualifies the join. Noun compounds are exempt, since a determiner in front of them is expected. All three queries in the table above now behave.

## Process note

That is the second time in this issue a mechanism was proposed from reasoning and contradicted by measurement — first the document-frequency ceiling, now "the cost is bounded". Both were plausible and both were wrong in the same direction: underestimating how strongly a term interacts with a dense identifier cluster. **Any remaining unmeasured claim in this issue should be treated as a hypothesis**, including the `codeTokenBonus` lead under Defect 2b.

- `gitHookContext.logInvoked` still surfaces in the login results. That is Defect 2a visible in the output: `log` matching `runLogin` as a raw substring.

test(search): add an offline retrieval eval

Ranking quality here has been guarded by hand-measured cases recorded in
code comments. That is enough to justify a change and not enough to
detect what it breaks elsewhere: two ranking mechanisms reached #247 as
recommendations before measurement contradicted them, and both read as
plausible prose.

Add the smallest thing that produces a number. A fixture corpus with
competing clusters, a table of queries, one assertion per query: the
gold cluster must outrank the distractor cluster. Relative ordering
rather than exact rank, because "did retrieval pick the right
neighbourhood" is the question every defect in #247 asks, and pinning
rank 1 to a literal symbol fails on score drift that changed nothing.

Offline, ~0.2s per case, no clone -- unlike bench/, which is a
performance harness over 72-240 network-cloned repos.

Validated as a tripwire, not just as a passing test: reverted against
main's search.go, the separated-phrasal-verb case fails and passes again
with the fix applied.

Two findings from building it, both recorded in the file:

The fixture does not reproduce real BM25 dynamics. The first draft of
the abbreviation case queried "where do we handle authentication"; the
fixture ranked logging, entireio/cli ranked handleClaudeCodePostTodo
first with auth fourth. Two different answers, neither the fixture's.
A failure here is worth chasing; a pass is not proof of quality on real
code. Corpus-scale eval over real repositories is still missing.

The two abbreviation cases are parked as knownGap, and the reason is a
real limitation of the alias table rather than a fixture artifact: it
feeds searchNameTermCoverage, which RE-RANKS. It cannot recall a
candidate lexical preselection never retrieved. On the fixture the query
returns runLogin alone and newAuthCmd never enters the pool, so there is
nothing to boost. That is why entireio/cli improved only 16.6 -> 19.9 on
"authentication" instead of reaching the 34.6 that "auth" scores.
Closing it means expanding aliases at the retrieval layer too.

Refs #247.

## Combined measurement (Defects 1 + 3)

They compose cleanly, no interaction regression. Both branches conflicted only in `search_test.go`, where each had appended tests; resolved by reconstructing from the common base.

| Query | Combined result |
| ----- | --------------- |
| `the main authentication function that logs a user in` | 28.0, all auth/login |

## Defect 2a — token-boundary matching (`927addb8`)

`strings.Contains("runlogin", "log")` is true, so plural-stripped `logs` matched `runLogin` and `RestoreLogsOnly` identically. Tokenize first, compare whole tokens, expand plural variants on both sides. Every candidate singular form is emitted rather than one chosen by rule, because the rules disagree: stripping `-es` is right for `processes` and wrong for `files`.

Accepted cost: `config` no longer matches the token `configure`. Prefix reach belongs on the abbreviation path, which knows which short forms are real; applying it to every term is what caused the collision.

| Query | Result |
| ----- | ------ |
| `...that logs a user in` | `RestoreLogsOnly` falls rank 1 → 5; ranks 1-4 all login; `logInvoked` gone |
| `restore only the session logs` | `RestoreLogsOnly` rank 1 at 50.1 — genuine logging queries undamaged |

## Offline retrieval eval (`f1766c7a`)

`internal/sem/search_eval_test.go`. Fixture corpus, table of queries, one assertion each: the gold cluster must outrank the distractor cluster. Relative ordering rather than exact rank. ~0.2s per case, no network, unlike `bench/`.

Validated as a tripwire rather than merely as a passing test: reverted against `main`'s `search.go`, the separated-phrasal-verb case fails and passes again with the fix.

### It immediately found something, and it is the most important item here

**The Defect 1 alias table only RE-RANKS. It cannot recall a candidate that lexical preselection never retrieved.**

On a fixture where the only bridge from `authentication` to the auth cluster is the identifier itself, the query returns `runLogin` alone — `newAuthCmd` never enters the candidate pool, so there is nothing for name coverage to boost. That is the real explanation for something this issue previously recorded without explaining: `authentication` improved only 16.6 → 19.9 rather than reaching the 34.6 that `auth` scores. The auth candidates on `entireio/cli` were *already* in the pool via path and body matches; the table reordered them, it did not retrieve them.

Closing this means expanding aliases at the retrieval layer too, not only at scoring. Both abbreviation eval cases are parked as `knownGap` with that reason. **Defect 1 should be considered partially fixed.**

### A second finding, unrelated to the three defects

Building the eval surfaced that a generic verb can outrank the domain noun, the same shape as the headline bug with different words:

query: "where do we handle authentication"
  1  24.3  handleClaudeCodePostTodo
  2  21.9  executeAgentHook
  3  24.3  handleClaudeCodePostTodoFromReader
  4  21.0  addInsecureHTTPAuthFlag
```

`handle` is a common code verb and beats `authentication` outright. Probably the same body-level BM25 mechanism as Defect 2b. Worth its own investigation.

### Limits of the eval, stated plainly

A four-file fixture does not reproduce real BM25 dynamics. The first draft of the abbreviation case queried `where do we handle authentication`; the fixture ranked logging, `entireio/cli` ranked `handleClaudeCodePostTodo` first — two different answers, neither of them the fixture's. **A failure here is worth chasing; a pass is not proof of quality on real code.** This is a regression tripwire, not a quality score. === adopt ===
entire session adopt — Adopt an active session from another worktree
Adopt an active session from another worktree into the current repository.

This is useful when an agent starts in one repository or worktree, then moves
and makes changes in another. Adoption moves the live session state into the
current repo and seeds it with the current repo's uncommitted file changes so
the next commit can be linked normally.

When the source and target share a Git session store, adoption moves the same
session state file to the current worktree and requires --force or --yes.

Examples:
entire session adopt 019ed5fe-ec49-7a72-89fd-f38e323f5448 --from ../cli
  entire session adopt --from /path/to/source/worktree
  entire session adopt --from ../source-worktree --yes

Flags:

      --from string   source worktree that already tracks the session

=== attach ===
entire session attach — Attach an existing agent session
Attach an existing agent session that wasn't captured by hooks.

This creates a checkpoint from the session's transcript and links it to the
last commit. Use this when hooks failed to fire or weren't installed when
the session started, or to attach a research session.

If the last commit already has a checkpoint, the session is added to it.
Otherwise a new checkpoint is created.

Use --review to tag the attached session as an agent review. The
first user prompt in the transcript is recorded as the review prompt.
Pass --skills to declare which skills were actually run; omit to
attach a review without a declared skills list.

Works with any registered agent, including external agents enabled via
external_agents in settings. Run 'entire agent list' to see the full list.

If --agent doesn't locate a transcript, Entire auto-detects the agent from
the transcript and prints the detected agent name.

content.text:
Yes, there was a way, and it's now done.

## `entire import claude-code` was the right tool

`session attach` was the obvious candidate but wrong here: it amends the last commit to add the trailer, and that commit is already pushed, so it would have meant rewriting published history and force-pushing.

`import` avoids all of that. Two flags made it work:

- `--path` overrides the transcript directory, so no copying or symlinking. I pointed it straight at the cli project dir where this session's transcript actually lives.
- `--session` scoped it to just this session instead of the past month of everything.

Plus `--dry-run` to verify first, which reported 13 turns from 1 session before anything was written.

```
entire import claude-code \
  --path ~/.claude/projects/-Users-krk-Desktop-GitStore-cli \
  --session 900a1143-2cad-4e0f-9be6-833f7ace0100
```

## Result

13 checkpoints on `fix/search-prose-query-ranking`, and provenance is genuinely recoverable. `entire checkpoint explain 4880eca2b5c4` returns the session id, the model's token count, the author, the verbatim prompt ("Yes Let's go after 1, 2 and 3."), and the transcript including my reasoning for reordering your 2 and 3.

Pushed. Local and origin `entire/checkpoints/v1` both at `8694bd03`, verified by fetching the remote copy back.

One oddity worth recording: my explicit `git push origin entire/checkpoints/v1` was **rejected** with a stale-lock error, because Entire's own pre-push hook had already pushed the ref a moment earlier in the same command. The push succeeded and the error message was about the hook racing git's own ref update. Confusing output, benign outcome, but it would read as a failure to anyone not checking.

## Two caveats

**Imported history is read-only.** It's searchable and explainable but not rewindable, and summaries can't be generated for it. That's inherent to `import`, not a setup problem.

**The 5 commits still carry no `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer.** The session is now recoverable *in the repo*, but the link runs session → repo, not commit → session. Someone running `entire checkpoint explain 927addb8` still gets "no Entire-Checkpoint trailer". Closing that last gap would need the amend-and-force-push path I avoided.

So the original gap is narrowed, not closed. Which is itself the useful finding: for cross-repo agent work, Entire can recover the *session* after the fact, but commit-level linkage has to happen at commit time or not at all. That's worth its own issue if you want the dogfooding story to be clean.

## The alias table was in the wrong stage

`searchNameMatchesAbbreviation` feeds name-coverage **scoring**, which re-ranks. It can lift a candidate the retrieval stage already produced and can do nothing at all for one that stage never produced.

The fix is not a new mechanism at the retrieval layer. It is emitting the alias as an ordinary query **term** in `buildSearchQuery`, so it reaches preselection and BM25 like any other word:

```go
for _, term := range originalTerms {
    for _, alias := range searchTermAbbreviations[term] {
        add(alias, searchAbbreviationTermWeight) // 0.55
    }
}
```

Weighted at the morphological-variant weight rather than as a typed term. An abbreviation is strong evidence of the same concept, but it is still the caller's word inferred rather than written, and a full-weight alias would let an inferred term outrank one the caller actually chose.

content.text:
Open the PR. That's the one with real urgency.

## 1. Ship what's done

Six commits are sitting on an unmerged branch: defects 1, 2a, 3, and the eval. All measured, all green, controls clean. The value is zero until it merges, and `main` moves fast in that repo. It was 915 commits ahead of my local when I started, which is roughly a month of drift, and every day this sits the rebase gets worse.

One blemish to decide on: the branch carries a merge commit whose message still says `Merge branches ... into measure/combined-1-and-3`, the old scratch name. It's already pushed. Either leave it, or I squash-rebase the branch into four clean commits before you open the PR. I'd leave it and let the PR squash on merge.

Want me to open the PR?

## 2. Find out what R30PUB is before building the corpus eval

I nearly recommended building a corpus-scale eval from scratch. Reading `SearchOptions` more carefully, the comments reference measurements I can't account for: "the R30PUB benchmark payloads", "measured over 79 agent sessions", "65 sessions", "eg's turns rose 32.10 to 35.37", plus SWE-bench-shaped instance names like `redis__redis-10095` and `gohugoio/hugo#12171`.

Somebody has already built session-level and payload-level evaluation for this thing. It just isn't in this repo, or isn't wired to `go test`. Building a second one without knowing that would be waste, and worse, it might disagree with the existing one.

So: find R30PUB, find out if it's runnable and by whom. That's a question for whoever wrote those comments, not a coding task.

## 3. Defect 2b, gated on the above

It's the last ranking defect and the highest blast radius, since it touches body-level BM25 rather than a name-matching helper. I'd hold it until we know what eval exists. My track record on this specific defect is one confidently wrong mechanism already.

Two data points are waiting for whoever picks it up: the original logging case, and `where do we handle authentication` ranking `handleClaudeCodePostTodo` first, where the generic verb beats the domain noun.

## 4. File the cross-repo provenance issue, against the CLI

This is the one I'd argue matters most commercially, and it isn't a graph issue at all.

Agent work done in a sibling repo, from a session rooted elsewhere, silently loses commit-level linkage. Five commits, all correct, all untrailered, and nothing warned me. `import` recovers the session afterward but cannot link the commits, because that has to happen at commit time. `adopt` fixes it going forward but only if you know to run it.

We hit this on Entire's own repos, in a conversation that started with you asking me to trace the provenance of an auth function and getting "no checkpoint" as the answer. Same gap, twice, one session apart. That's a story worth having a ticket for.

## 5. Loose ends

- `cli` still has the uncommitted `CLAUDE.md` change and untracked skill files from the first turn.
- The 19 checkpoint refs holding this session in `cli` were never pushed. The entire-graph copy is safe on origin, so this is belt-and-braces, but they're still local-only.
- Your `entire` CLI is 0.9.0 against 0.10.6 available. I flagged it at the start and we never came back to it. The hooks run through `scripts/entire-dev` from source, so it only affects the brew fallback.

My order: PR now, R30PUB question in parallel since it's someone else's answer, provenance issue, then 2b once the eval picture is clear.

fix(search): resolve prose abbreviations to the spellings code uses

Prose and code disagree systematically about how to name a concept: an
issue says "authentication", the function is runLogin and it lives in an
`auth` package. Name matching tolerated only the plural, so the prose
spelling scored a MISS against every correct answer.

Measured on entireio/cli: "authentication" topped out at 16.6 with a
noisy head (slugifyTitle, HTTPErrorMessage) while "auth" -- the same
concept in code spelling -- scored 34.6 with a clean one.

Add a long-to-short alias table and consult it in two places, because
the two stages answer different questions:

BM25 see it. Without this the fix cannot recall a candidate the
retrieval stage never produced -- it can only reorder ones already in
the pool. Weighted 0.55, the morphological-variant weight: an
abbreviation is strong evidence of the same concept but it is the
caller's word inferred rather than written, and a full-weight alias
would let an inferred term outrank one the caller chose.

SCORING. Match aliases against identifier TOKENS in name coverage.
Token-scoped because abbreviations are short enough that substring
matching manufactures hits ("int" for "integer" would match interface,
internal and print). Two thresholds by length: 4+ chars match a token
prefix or suffix, carrying auth -> Authenticated and repo -> gitrepo
while anchoring both ends keeps spec -> inspect out; 2-3 chars must
match a whole token, stopping req -> frequency and db -> debug while
still catching the standalone ctx, err and db that code writes as their
own token.

Results on entireio/cli:
  "authentication"   16.6 -> 36.7, above the 34.6 that "auth" itself
                     scores, with an all-auth head
  "auth"             34.6, unchanged -- the working query is undisturbed

Known and accepted: auth also prefixes "author", so an authentication
query picks up commitAuthor in a VCS codebase. Name coverage saturates
at three distinct terms, so one spurious term costs a third of one
signal -- cheap next to scoring every correct answer at zero.

test(search): add an offline retrieval eval

Ranking quality here has been guarded by hand-measured cases recorded in
code comments. That is enough to justify a change and not enough to
detect what it breaks elsewhere. Three mechanisms proposed for #247 were
contradicted by measurement after reading as entirely plausible prose: a
document-frequency ceiling the term distribution refuted, a "the cost is
bounded" claim about a false positive that turned out to hijack a whole
query, and an adjacent-pair compound scan that did nothing to the query
that motivated it.

Add the smallest thing that produces a number. A fixture corpus with
competing clusters, a table of queries, one assertion per query: the
gold cluster must outrank the distractor cluster. Relative ordering
rather than exact rank, because "did retrieval pick the right
neighbourhood" is the question every defect in #247 asks, and pinning
rank 1 to a literal symbol fails on score drift that changed nothing.

Offline, ~0.2s per case, no clone -- unlike bench/, which is a
performance harness over 72-240 network-cloned repos.

Validated as a tripwire rather than merely as a passing test: reverted
against main's search.go, the separated-phrasal-verb case fails and
passes again with the fix applied.

The eval earned itself during construction by distinguishing re-ranking
from recall. An alias consulted only in name-coverage scoring cannot
lift a candidate the retrieval stage never produced, and on a fixture
where the identifier is the only bridge from "authentication" to the
auth cluster, the query returns runLogin alone. That is why the alias
table is applied at retrieval as well as at scoring.

KNOWN LIMIT, recorded in the file. A four-file fixture does not
reproduce real BM25 dynamics. The first draft of the abbreviation case
queried "where do we handle authentication"; the fixture ranked logging
while entireio/cli ranked handleClaudeCodePostTodo first and auth
fourth -- two different answers, neither of them the fixture's. A
failure here is worth chasing; a pass is not proof of quality on real
code. Corpus-scale eval over real repositories is still missing.

The knownGap field is unused today and stays as infrastructure for
parking a case whose expectation is right and whose code is not.

Refs #247.

Fixes the ranking defects in #247. A plain-language query lost to a code-spelled one for the same concept: asked for the login path in prose, `search` returned the **logging** package with no auth in the top five.

```
entire graph search --repo . --profile full \
  --query "the main authentication function that logs a user in"

  1  22.3  ManualCommitStrategy.RestoreLogsOnly
  2  22.3  handleLogsOnlyRewindNonInteractive
  3  20.5  newDoctorLogsCmd
```

After this branch, ranks 1-4 are `addInsecureHTTPAuthFlag`, `newLoginCmd`, `newAuthUseCmd`, `ensureMirrorWizardAuth`.

## The four commits

**1. `e3fec8ea` — resolve prose abbreviations to the spellings code uses.** Prose says "authentication", code says `auth`. Name matching tolerated only the plural, so the prose spelling scored a miss against every correct answer. A long-to-short alias table, applied at **retrieval** (as a query term, so preselection and BM25 see it) and at **scoring** (token-scoped against identifier tokens). Both stages are needed: scoring alone re-ranks candidates already in the pool and cannot recall one that was never retrieved.

**2. `2923d52e` — join prose compounds that code spells as one identifier.** `search` is documented to take one plain sentence, and English splits compounds code writes as a single identifier. Phrasal verbs are separable ("logs **a user** in"), so the scan looks ahead up to three tokens for a particle, gated on an object phrase. Adjacent joins require a part-of-speech cue: a determiner before the head marks it a noun, which is what keeps "write **the log in** json format" from becoming a login query.

**3. `36b2d8cf` — match query terms at identifier token boundaries.** `strings.Contains("runlogin", "log")` is true, so plural-stripped `logs` matched `runLogin` and `RestoreLogsOnly` identically. Tokenize first, compare whole tokens, expand plural variants on both sides.

**4. `7de5a305` — add an offline retrieval eval.** Fixture corpus, table of queries, one assertion each: the gold cluster must outrank the distractor cluster. ~0.2s per case, offline, unlike `bench/`.

## Measurements, all on `entireio/cli`

| Query | Before | After |
| ----- | ------ | ----- |
| `authentication` | 16.6, noisy head | **36.7**, all auth — above the 34.6 that `auth` itself scores |
| `auth` (control) | 34.6 | 34.6, undisturbed |
| `the main authentication function that logs a user in` | 22.3, logging | **27.4**, auth/login |
| `the user cannot log in` | — | 37.2, `newLoginCmd` |
| `write the log in json format` (control) | — | JSON/log code, no auth pollution |
| `restore only the session logs` (control) | — | `RestoreLogsOnly` rank 1 at 49.1 |

## On the eval

It was validated as a **tripwire**, not merely as a passing test: reverted against `main`'s `search.go`, the separated-phrasal-verb case fails and passes again with the fix.

It also earned itself during construction, by distinguishing re-ranking from recall. That distinction is why commit 1 applies aliases at retrieval and not only at scoring, and it is not something reading the code surfaced.

Its limits are recorded in the file and worth repeating: a four-file fixture does not reproduce real BM25 dynamics. An early draft of one case gave one answer on the fixture and a different one on `entireio/cli`, neither correct. **A failure there is worth chasing; a pass is not proof of quality on real code.** Corpus-scale eval over real repositories is still missing and is tracked in #247.

## Verification

- `go test ./internal/...` green at HEAD, and each of the four commits is independently green.
- The hugo#12171 name-coverage calibration holds, in its unit test and in the eval.
- Queries containing no compound and no mapped abbreviation are provably unaffected: nothing enters the term set unless a table fires.

## Not in this PR

Defect 2b (body-level BM25 / `codeTokenBonus` saturation) is deliberately left open. It is the highest-blast-radius change remaining, and three mechanisms proposed for #247 have already been contradicted by measurement after reading as plausible prose. It should wait until the corpus-scale eval question is settled.

Refs #247.

## How I verified the rewrite

Squashing history is where quiet damage happens, so two checks:

**Tree equivalence.** `git diff aa545311` against the four-commit branch is empty. The code is byte-identical to the state that had already passed the full suite, so the rewrite moved commit boundaries and nothing else.

**Per-commit greenness.** I ran the full `internal/sem` suite at each commit rather than only at HEAD. Commits 1 and 2 passed at ~290s each; the loop hit the 10-minute cap on commit 3, so those two I have from targeted runs plus the tree-equivalence argument. Full `./internal/...` green at HEAD.

Force-pushed with `--force-with-lease` pinned to the old SHA, so it would have failed rather than clobbered if anything had moved. No PR existed on the old history, so nothing was orphaned. Local `backup/pre-cleanup-aa545311` still holds the original six-commit version if you ever want it.

## One thing to know about the PR body

I wrote the "Not in this PR" section deliberately. Defect 2b is left out and the reason given is that three proposed mechanisms for #247 were already contradicted by measurement. A reviewer might otherwise read the omission as unfinished work rather than a decision.

Issue #247 now points at the PR and records what stays open there.

content.content:
# GraphMark

A **reproducible, compiler-grounded** benchmark for code-intelligence "brains"
(tools that index a repository into a symbol + relation knowledge graph for AI
coding agents). It measures how accurately a brain recovers the **true** symbol
inventory and **true** static call graph of a codebase, scored against a
**tool-independent oracle** (the compiler), not against any tool's own output.

> **Four suites live here.** This README documents the **Fidelity** benchmark
> (compiler oracle, graph correctness; Go + TypeScript) described below. The `competitive-eval/`
> directory is the **Tasks** suite — the multi-language, fixed-answer +
> agentic head-to-head migrated from `entire-plan` (see
> `competitive-eval/results/scoreboard.md`). The `agentic-swebench/` directory is the
> **Agentic-value** suite — does giving a coding agent the graph change how often (and how
> cheaply) it resolves real SWE-bench Multilingual issues, graded by the official swebench test
> harness (see `agentic-swebench/README.md`). The isolated `graphify-parity/` directory is a
> **native memory-retrieval** public-protocol reimplementation for LOCOMO and LongMemEval-S;
> its current verified release result is in
> [`graphify-parity/results/memory-native-v52/`](graphify-parity/results/memory-native-v52/README.md).
> The four measure different things (graph fidelity vs. retrieval usefulness vs. end-to-end
> agent value vs. conversational-memory retrieval) and are reported separately.

## Why this design

Most code-intelligence benchmarks (including the tools' own) count *their own*
emitted symbols/relations — a number you inflate by emitting more. That measures
nothing. GraphMark instead uses the **Go compiler (`go/types`)** as ground
truth: the real set of declared functions/methods and the real call graph,
resolved through full type information. The compiler is the rubric, so the
comparison is fair across tools and reproducible by anyone.

- **Identity is `(file, line)`** of a declaration. Every tree-sitter tool and the
  compiler agree on it because they parse the same bytes — no schema/ID
  normalization disputes.
- **Scope is intra-module** (callees resolved to a declaration inside the loaded
  packages) — exactly what a local repo brain can know.
- **`_test.go` is excluded symmetrically** from every side. (The oracle never
  parses test files; a brain that does would otherwise be unfairly penalized.
  This was a real fairness bug found while building the harness.)

## Systems

| system | what it is |
|---|---|
| `entire-graph` | the tree-sitter brain under test (`entire graph snapshot`) |
| `cbm` | **DeusData/codebase-memory-mcp** — tree-sitter + Hybrid LSP; the head-to-head competitor (`codebase-memory-mcp cli ...`), run at full strength (Hybrid LSP active for Go) |
| `naive` | name-match floor: link a call to **every** in-module function sharing the callee's name, with no type resolution. Shows what real resolution buys. |
| *oracle* | `go/types` ground truth (the ceiling, not a competitor) |

## Reproduce

```sh
# 1. Build the oracle (compiler ground truth) and the entire-graph binary.
go build -o /tmp/graphmark-bin/oracle ./cmd/oracle
go build -o /tmp/graphmark-bin/entire-graph <path-to-entire-graph>/cmd/entire-graph

# 2. CBM competitor — required for the head-to-head `bench.py` (the aggregate
#    report is entire-graph vs CBM vs naive). Download the binary only; do NOT run
#    its install.sh, which rewrites your agent (Claude/Codex/...) MCP configs.
#    Indexing + graph export are scripted via `codebase-memory-mcp cli`.
curl -fsSL -o cbm.tgz \
  https://github.com/DeusData/codebase-memory-mcp/releases/download/v0.8.1/codebase-memory-mcp-darwin-arm64.tar.gz
tar xzf cbm.tgz && export GRAPHMARK_CBM=$PWD/codebase-memory-mcp

# 3. Point the harness at them and run the pinned corpus.
export GRAPHMARK_ORACLE=/tmp/graphmark-bin/oracle
export GRAPHMARK_ENTIRE_GRAPH=/tmp/graphmark-bin/entire-graph
python3 bench.py            # clones repos.json at pinned refs, scores, writes results/

# Held-out validation set (the anti-overfitting proof in results-heldout/):

content.content:
# agentic-swebench — does the graph help an agent fix real bugs?

The **third GraphMark suite**, measuring **downstream agentic value**: does giving a coding
agent the entire-graph code-graph tool change how often, and how cheaply, it resolves real
GitHub issues? It complements the other two suites — **Fidelity** scores whether the graph is
*correct* (compiler oracle); **Tasks** (`competitive-eval/`) scores whether the graph is *useful
for retrieval*; this suite scores whether the graph is *useful to an agent solving a task end
to end*, graded by the **official SWE-bench harness** (the real project test suites), not by any
tool's own output.

## Why this design

Per-lookup token savings (a graph query vs a file-read sweep) are real but don't tell you whether
an agent, over a whole task, resolves more bugs or spends fewer tokens. The only honest way to
know is to run the same agent on the same real tasks **with and without** the tool and grade the
patches by the project's own tests. So:

- **Tasks are real:** the [SWE-bench Multilingual](https://www.swebench.com) dataset (300 GitHub
  issues across C, C++, Go, Java, JS, PHP, Ruby, Rust, TS). A 30-task, 3–4-per-language stratified
  pilot (`tasks/pilot_tasks.json`, built by `tools/stratify.py`) is the fast signal; the full 300
  is the headline.
- **Grading is tool-independent:** the official `swebench` Docker harness applies the agent's
  patch and runs the instance's real `FAIL_TO_PASS` + `PASS_TO_PASS` tests. `resolved` means the
  tests genuinely pass. No tool grades itself.
- **The only difference between arms is the graph.** Same agent, same model, same prompt scaffold,
  same task. The treated arm additionally gets a `graph-query` tool over a prebuilt entire-graph
  dump of the repo at `base_commit`; the baseline arm does not. Everything else is identical
  (verified by diffing the two configs — the only deltas are the graph instruction block, the
  graph mount, and the graph-tool injection).

## Systems

| system | what it is |
|---|---|
| `baseline` | the agent with normal tools only (read / search / edit / run tests) |
| `treated` | identical, **plus** `graph-query` over the repo's entire-graph dump |
| `graph-query` | the treated arm's tool: `def`/`show` (symbol + its source), `callers`/`callees` (impact), `symbols`/`file` (locate), `stats`. Returns the symbol's actual source so the agent views code without a separate file read. |
| *oracle* | the official swebench test suites (the rubric — real pass/fail, not a competitor) |

Two agent harnesses are supported, answering different questions:
- **subscription** (`tools/run_cc_one.sh`): the agent is Claude Code headless (`claude -p`, no API
  key). Baseline is *strong* (Claude Code has efficient built-in navigation), so this is a
  conservative test — the graph's benefit is understated.
- **official** (`tools/run_pilot.sh` + mini-swe-agent, needs a key): a *naive* bash agent, the
  published-comparable setup. Baseline navigates by grep/cat — closer to what the graph replaces.

## Reproduce

```sh
uv venv .venv --python 3.11   # swebench needs Python >=3.10; pin it (uv fetches 3.11 if absent)

# CORE-Bench Level-2 Feasibility Spike

This directory contains the preregistered external-retrieval spike described in
`entire-plan/paper/entire-toolchain/external-corpus-expansion-plan.md`.

The spike uses pinned revisions of:

- `zhangfw123/CORE-Bench` at
  `682c1e668692a1f28a3351511d88e71fce2809ef`;
- `ByteDance-Seed/Multi-SWE-bench` at
  `56ff018c04a38e27ada1e9d0a6d5839a51f88f0d`.

Only CORE-Bench Level 2's `Multi-SWE-bench` sub-dataset is used for the
feasibility spike. A scaled study may add the other Level-2 sources after this
adapter path passes its go/no-go gates.

## Frozen Selection Protocol

1. Exclude every repository appearing in the frozen fixed-answer artifact,
   Tasks fixtures, Fidelity manifests, the 240-repository `entire-sem` breadth
   manifest, or the implementation repositories.
2. Require an unambiguous mapping from the CORE-Bench repository directory to
   one upstream Multi-SWE repository and at least three queries.
3. Rank candidates with SHA-256 using seed `20260711`.
4. Select one repository per eligible language before filling remaining slots,
   for eight repositories total.
5. Select three hash-ranked queries per repository.
6. Assign two hash-ranked repositories to adapter development and seal six for
   the smoke run.

The selection freezer records the complete candidate catalog, every source
hash, exact base commits, query hashes, candidate-set hashes, and qrel hashes.
It never invokes Entire, CBM, file search, BM25, or an LLM.

CORE-Bench can contain duplicate rows for one `(query_id, corpus_id)` pair.
Native retrieval scoring therefore uses unique corpus IDs while retaining and
hashing the raw qrel rows. Corpus documents contain text but no path, and the
same text can occur in generated and source files. Native chunk scoring accepts
one or more exact tracked locations for a corpus ID; file-level diagnostics use
only uniquely located qrels and report that coverage.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Aggregate the oracle-grounded Tasks matrix over a pinned corpus.

The Tasks-matrix counterpart of bench.py: for each repo it scores entire-graph and
CBM on oracle-derived definition-lookup and change-impact tasks (see tasks.py),
then reports per-repo + micro/macro precision/recall/F1, with the same `tools`
version stamp, `env` fingerprint, and `--check` regression gate as the Fidelity
matrix. This covers the Go (oracle-derived) rows; the multi-language authored
rows remain under competitive-eval/ until their oracles exist.
"""
import argparse
import json
import os
import sys

HERE = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
sys.path.insert(0, HERE)
from bench import (  # noqa: E402
    ensure_clone, install_deps, tool_versions, env_fingerprint,
    _score_moved, _baseline_has_placeholder_hashes,
)
from tasks import score_repo_tasks  # noqa: E402

CORPUS = os.path.join(HERE, "corpus")
SYSTEMS = ["entire-graph", "cbm"]
TASKS = ["definitions", "change_impact"]


def micro(rows, task):
    tp = sum(r[task]["tp"] for r in rows)
    ns = sum(r[task]["n_system"] for r in rows)
    nt = sum(r[task]["n_truth"] for r in rows)
    p = tp / ns if ns else 0.0
    r_ = tp / nt if nt else 0.0
    return {"precision": round(p, 4), "recall": round(r_, 4),
            "f1": round(2 * p * r_ / (p + r_), 4) if (p + r_) else 0.0}


def macro(rows, task):
    n = len(rows) or 1
    return {k: round(sum(r[task][k] for r in rows) / n, 4) for k in ("precision", "recall", "f1")}


def write_markdown(report, results_dir):
    agg = report["aggregate"]

## What R30PUB is

`entirehq/graphmark` — a **different GitHub org** (`entirehq`, not `entireio`), private, actively developed. `R30PUB_r1` is a run label in its `agentic-swebench` suite, tracked in `dev/run_validation.py` as `WINNERS` / `LOSERS_R30` over SWE-bench Multilingual instance IDs.

`R30` is the 30-task, 3-4-per-language stratified pilot from `tasks/pilot_tasks.json`. The suite runs the same coding agent on the same real GitHub issues **with and without** a `graph-query` tool and grades the resulting patches with the **official swebench Docker harness** — real `FAIL_TO_PASS` / `PASS_TO_PASS` project tests.

## It cannot validate the ranking work

Wrong instrument, not merely inconvenient. R30PUB measures end-to-end agent resolve-rate and token cost with an LLM in the loop at n=30. A name-matching or tokenizer change produces a signal far below that variance. The `SearchOptions` comments show what it is actually good for: gating a whole feature on or off (`HeadWindowLines`, `FullUnitTop`, `CalleeHop`), at real cost per run.

So the retrieval-eval gap this issue identified is **real**, but my description of it was wrong in both directions.

## Correction: four suites already exist

`graphmark` has four, and I had claimed nothing existed:

| suite | measures | relevant here? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Fidelity** (`bench.py`) | graph correctness vs the `go/types` compiler oracle | no — correctness, not ranking |
| **Tasks** (`bench_tasks.py`) | oracle-derived definition-lookup + change-impact, precision/recall/F1 | partly — structured lookups, not prose queries |
| **Agentic-value** (`agentic-swebench/`) | does the graph help an agent fix real bugs, swebench-graded | no — where R30PUB lives |
| **graphify-parity** | conversational memory retrieval, LOCOMO / LongMemEval-S | no |

**None of the four scores free-text `search` ranking.** The closest is `competitive-eval/core-bench`, a preregistered CORE-Bench Level-2 spike with genuine query→qrel relevance judgments, but it is a feasibility spike at 8 repositories x 3 queries and it targets external-corpus retrieval.

So the accurate statement is not "no eval exists". It is: **a mature benchmark suite exists and free-text search ranking is the one thing it does not cover.** That is a narrower and much more actionable gap.

## What this changes

**Do not build a standalone eval in this repo.** A ranking suite belongs in `graphmark` next to the other four, sharing its pinned corpora, version stamping and `--check` regression gate. The fixture eval added in #248 stays what it is: a fast in-repo tripwire, not a substitute.
