## Reproduce

```sh
# 1. Build the oracle (compiler ground truth) and the entire-graph binary.
go build -o /tmp/graphmark-bin/oracle ./cmd/oracle
go build -o /tmp/graphmark-bin/entire-graph <path-to-entire-graph>/cmd/entire-graph

# 2. CBM competitor — required for the head-to-head `bench.py` (the aggregate
#    report is entire-graph vs CBM vs naive). Download the binary only; do NOT run
#    its install.sh, which rewrites your agent (Claude/Codex/...) MCP configs.
#    Indexing + graph export are scripted via `codebase-memory-mcp cli`.
curl -fsSL -o cbm.tgz \
  https://github.com/DeusData/codebase-memory-mcp/releases/download/v0.8.1/codebase-memory-mcp-darwin-arm64.tar.gz
tar xzf cbm.tgz && export GRAPHMARK_CBM=$PWD/codebase-memory-mcp

# 3. Point the harness at them and run the pinned corpus.
export GRAPHMARK_ORACLE=/tmp/graphmark-bin/oracle
export GRAPHMARK_ENTIRE_GRAPH=/tmp/graphmark-bin/entire-graph
python3 bench.py            # clones repos.json at pinned refs, scores, writes results/

# Held-out validation set (the anti-overfitting proof in results-heldout/):
python3 bench.py --manifest repos-heldout.json --out results-heldout

# Single repo, single system — the only CBM-free path (no GRAPHMARK_CBM needed):
python3 run.py corpus/mux --system entire-graph
```

`repos.json` pins each repository to a tag; `bench.py` records the resolved SHA.
Cloned sources live under `corpus/` (gitignored). Results land in `results/`.

## Validated against GraphMark — no collateral regression

Ran the `entirehq/graphmark` **Fidelity** and **Tasks** suites over their pinned 18-repository Go corpus, with two binaries built from this repo: `main` (`a8ae590f`) and this branch (`7de5a305`). Same oracle, same corpus at pinned refs, same harness.

**Zero metric differences.** Not "within noise" — byte-identical across all 18 repos and every metric.

Fidelity (graph correctness vs the `go/types` compiler oracle), micro-averaged:

| metric | main | this branch |
| --- | --- | --- |
| symbols P/R/F1 | 0.9407 / 1.0000 / 0.9695 | 0.9407 / 1.0000 / 0.9695 |
| calls_all P/R/F1 | 0.8406 / 0.8334 / 0.8370 | 0.8406 / 0.8334 / 0.8370 |
| calls_exact_only P/R/F1 | 0.9899 / 0.2026 / 0.3364 | 0.9899 / 0.2026 / 0.3364 |

Tasks (oracle-derived lookups), micro-averaged:

| task | main | this branch |
| --- | --- | --- |
| definitions P/R/F1 | 0.9632 / 1.0000 / 0.9813 | 0.9632 / 1.0000 / 0.9813 |
| change_impact P/R/F1 | 0.9896 / 0.8521 / 0.9157 | 0.9896 / 0.8521 / 0.9157 |

Corpus: httprouter, mux, errors, pflag, uuid, websocket, logrus, color, chi, go-cmp, mapstructure, xxhash, multierror, zerolog, cobra, testify, jwt, ulid — each at its pinned tag.

### What this does and does not establish

**Does:** the changes are confined to search ranking. Identical rather than merely close numbers is the strong form of that claim — symbol extraction, call-graph construction, definition lookup and change-impact are provably untouched.

**Does not:** validate the ranking improvements themselves. Grepping the harnesses for the subcommands they invoke returns `symbols`, `stats` and `snapshot` only. **Neither suite ever calls `search`.** So this is a clean negative control, not evidence the ranking got better.

Evidence for the improvement remains the hand measurements in the commit messages and the fixture eval in `7de5a305`. GraphMark has four suites and free-text search ranking is the one thing none of them scores; that gap is tracked in #247, and it belongs in graphmark rather than here.

Reproduce:

```sh
go build -o /tmp/graphmark-bin/oracle ./cmd/oracle          # in graphmark
export GRAPHMARK_ORACLE=/tmp/graphmark-bin/oracle
export GRAPHMARK_ENTIRE_GRAPH=<binary under test>
python3 run.py corpus/<repo> --system entire-graph --json out.json
```

`run.py --system entire-graph` is the CBM-free path, so the head-to-head competitor binary is not needed for a main-versus-branch comparison.

content.text:
Validated. **Zero metric differences**, identical rather than merely close.

## What ran

Cloned `entirehq/graphmark`, built its compiler oracle, and built two entire-graph binaries: `main` (`a8ae590f`) and the PR branch (`7de5a305`). Ran both suites over graphmark's pinned 18-repo Go corpus, same oracle, same refs.

**Fidelity** (graph correctness vs `go/types`), micro-averaged:

| metric | main | branch |
|---|---|---|
| symbols P/R/F1 | 0.9407 / 1.0000 / 0.9695 | identical |
| calls_all | 0.8406 / 0.8334 / 0.8370 | identical |
| calls_exact_only | 0.9899 / 0.2026 / 0.3364 | identical |

**Tasks** (oracle-derived lookups):

| task | main | branch |
|---|---|---|
| definitions | 0.9632 / 1.0000 / 0.9813 | identical |
| change_impact | 0.9896 / 0.8521 / 0.9157 | identical |

Zero differences across 18 repos and every field, not just the aggregates.

## What it proves, and what it doesn't

**Proves:** the changes are confined to search ranking. Identical numbers are the strong form of that. Symbol extraction, call-graph construction, definition lookup and change-impact are provably untouched.

**Doesn't prove the ranking got better.** I grepped the harnesses for which subcommands they actually invoke: `symbols`, `stats`, `snapshot`. Nothing else. **Neither suite ever calls `search`.**

So this is a clean negative control and nothing more. It was still worth running, because "we changed the ranker and nothing else moved" is exactly the claim a reviewer can't take on faith, but it isn't evidence the fix works. That still rests on the hand measurements in the commit messages and the fixture eval.

It also confirms the gap in #247 from a second direction: a ranking change genuinely cannot be measured by anything that exists today.

## Two practical notes

`run.py --system entire-graph` is the CBM-free path, so the competitor binary was never needed for a main-versus-branch comparison. That's the cheap route for any future PR, about 2.5s per repo, roughly 90 seconds for the whole matrix.

Cleanup: temporary worktree removed, branch and session intact. Graphmark is now cloned at `/Users/krk/Desktop/GitStore/graphmark` (301MB with its corpus) if you want it.

Posted to both PR #248 and issue #247, with the "never calls search" caveat stated explicitly in each so nobody reads zero-difference as validation of the improvement.

Remaining: the ranking suite in graphmark, the cross-reference so R30PUB citations are reproducible, and defect 2b once there's something to measure it with.

content.text:
The oracle already exists. That's the whole plan, really.

## The key finding

`agentic-swebench/tasks/multilingual_300.json` has 300 instances, each carrying both halves of a retrieval eval:

- **`problem_statement`** is natural-language issue text. That is the query, written by a human who did not know the codebase's naming.
- **`patch`** is the gold human fix. The files and lines it touches are the correct answer.

No labeling effort, no LLM, no Docker. The ground truth is a real developer's real fix, which satisfies graphmark's house rule that no tool grades itself. `test_patch` is stored separately, so `patch` is source-only, which matters because test files are excluded symmetrically elsewhere in graphmark.

This is also the same data behind the "8 of 12 code-gold files were ranked" line in `search_callee.go`. Somebody already computed this by hand. The plan is to make it a suite.

## Metrics

Two families, matching vocabulary the repo already uses:

| metric | question | oracle needed |
|---|---|---|
| file recall@1/5/10 | is a gold file ranked | none, comes straight from the patch |
| MRR over gold files | how far down | none |
| symbol recall@k | is the symbol containing a changed line ranked | yes |
| editability | are the gold lines actually printed | yes |

The split matters. **File-level gold is oracle-free**, so it works across all nine languages immediately. Symbol-level needs to map hunk lines to declarations, which only works where graphmark has an oracle (Go, TypeScript, Python). So file-level is the headline metric and symbol-level is the deeper cut on a language subset.

Add a **naive floor**, matching graphmark's existing style: BM25 over files, or grep for the query's rare terms. Without it the numbers say nothing about what the graph buys over plain text search.

## The part that decides whether this is worth anything

I hand-tuned an alias table by eyeballing `entireio/cli`. If the suite is built and tuned on the same instances it reports, the numbers are self-congratulatory.

So it needs a **sealed held-out split from day one**, mirroring `repos-heldout.json` and the CORE-Bench spike's protocol: SHA-256 hash-ranked selection under a fixed seed, one slice for development, the rest sealed. Tuning happens on dev, the headline is reported on held-out, and the seal is recorded in the manifest. That convention already exists in this repo; the ranking suite should just inherit it.

## Phases

**Phase 0, before writing anything.** Two questions. Does `agentic-swebench` already keep repo checkouts at `base_commit` and prebuilt graph dumps? Its README implies the treated arm needs exactly that, and if it exists the corpus problem is already solved. And is the script that produced the "8 of 12" number sitting in `dev/`? Worth ten minutes before building.

**Phase 1.** File-level recall and MRR on the 30-instance pilot, entire-graph versus naive floor. Deliberately small. This produces the first real number and will expose whatever I have wrong about query construction.

**Phase 2.** Symbol-level and editability for Go, TypeScript and Python, reusing the oracle binaries already built.

**Phase 3.** Scale to 300, seal the held-out split, wire up `bench.py`'s conventions: `tools` version stamp, `env` fingerprint, committed baseline, `--check` regression gate. At that point it is a peer of the other suites and can gate PRs.

**Phase 4.** Use it to settle defect 2b, which is the first change that genuinely should not ship on hand measurement.

## Risks I would state up front

**Issue text is not a search query.** Problem statements are verbose, with stack traces and repro steps; real queries are a sentence. The suite measures a proxy. Mitigation: report title-only and full-statement as two separate conditions. Title-only is much closer to real query shape, and the gap between the two conditions is itself informative.

**One query per instance.** 300 queries is thin by IR standards, and they cluster by repo. Fine for regression detection, weak for fine-grained tuning. The CORE-Bench spike with real qrels is the natural complement later.

**Query construction biases everything.** Whatever recipe turns `problem_statement` into a query has to be fixed, documented, and hashed into the manifest before any tuning, or it becomes a knob someone tunes.

## Where it lives

A new suite directory in graphmark, reusing `bench.py`'s `ensure_clone`, `tool_versions`, `env_fingerprint` and `--check` rather than reimplementing them. Not in entire-graph. The fixture eval in PR #248 stays what it is, a sub-second in-repo tripwire.

Worth noting what this would have caught: all three mechanisms I got wrong this session were single-query judgments. A 30-query suite kills all three in minutes.

Want me to run Phase 0 and then build Phase 1?

content.text:
Thomas Dohmke pushed three commits to the branch last night (22:26 to 22:48 CEST), all from Entire-tracked Codex sessions. He found two real bugs in my work.

## Bug 1: plural queries never reached the alias table

My retrieval loop iterated `originalTerms`, a snapshot taken **before** morphological expansion, then did an exact lookup `searchTermAbbreviations[term]`. So a plural long-form query never matched a table key. `searchNameMatchesAbbreviation` had the identical exact-key problem.

Measured on `entireio/cli`, my build vs his:

| Query | Mine | His |
|---|---|---|
| `configurations` | 10.4 `Configured`, then noise | **26.5** `LoadCheckpointsConfig`, `Config`, `globalConfigDirPath` |
| `repositories` | 35.4 | **41.1**, same hits, alias now firing |

`configurations` was returning essentially nothing. His `searchAbbreviations()` runs `searchNameWordVariants` before the lookup and he moved the snapshot to after morphology, so inferred singular and verb forms participate. Covers `-ies` too: `repositories` to `repository` to `repo`.

## Bug 2: my determiner guard fixed one instance, not the class

This one stings. My commit message claimed the determiner cue handled noun-plus-preposition, and I verified it on `write the log in json format`. I never tried the case where `log` really is a verb:

```
"log a message in json format"
  mine    29.6 newLoginCmd,  29.1 RecordLoginContext
  thomas  28.8 log,  28.4 formatMessageSuffix
```

The exact false positive I declared fixed, still there. A determiner before the head only catches `the log`; it does nothing when the object sits between verb and particle.

His `searchCompoundFormatPreposition` checks whether `in` is followed by a format name or a word before `format`/`encoding`. The two-commit refinement is the interesting part: scoped to `login` on the adjacent path, applied to every verb on the separated path. The reasoning in his comment is that in the separated case the object already precedes `in`, so a trailing format describes that object for any verb ("sign the request in JSON"), whereas adjacent "check in a JSON file" puts the object *after* `in` and must still join. His tests pin both directions, including `log the user in and return JSON` still returning login.

## State

Fast-forwarded to `f52f6088`. Full `./internal/...` green, exit 0. The eval is now six cases with his `plural configuration reaches config` added, all passing.

## The thing worth saying

That is the third time this session I generalised from a single measured example: the DF ceiling, "the cost is bounded", and now the determiner guard. Same failure mode each time, and each time the commit message stated the general claim while the evidence covered one instance.

The fixture eval I built did not catch either bug, because I wrote its cases from the same examples I used to write the code. Thomas's additions are the cases I lacked the imagination for. That is a decent argument that the ranking suite matters less for its regression gate than for supplying queries nobody on the team would think to write, which is exactly what SWE-bench `problem_statement` text gives you for free.

Want me to update PR #248 with the corrected claims, since its description still says the determiner guard handles the false positive?

## Correction: two claims in the description were wrong

@ashtom pushed `1bd66098`, `51a1628e` and `f52f6088` fixing two real defects in the first four commits. Recording the corrections visibly rather than only editing the description, since the description asserted one of these as fixed when it was not.

### 1. The determiner cue did not fix the false positive, it fixed one instance of it

The description for `2923d52e` claimed a determiner before the head was the part-of-speech cue that keeps a logging query from becoming a login query. It catches `write **the log** in json`. It does nothing when `log` is genuinely a verb and its object sits between verb and particle:

```
query: "log a message in json format"          (before f52f6088)
  1  29.6  newLoginCmd
  2  29.1  RecordLoginContext
```

The exact false positive the commit message declared fixed, still present in a form I did not test. I verified the one example I had written the guard from, then generalised from it.

`searchCompoundFormatPreposition` is the actual fix: reject the join when `in` introduces an output format (`json`, `yaml`, …, or any word followed by `format`/`encoding`) rather than completing a phrasal verb. After it, the same query returns `log` and `formatMessageSuffix`.

The scoping across `51a1628e` and `f52f6088` is the part worth reading. A defect in `e3fec8ea` and `aa545311` (now folded into `e3fec8ea`). The retrieval loop iterated `originalTerms`, a snapshot taken **before** the morphological expansion ran, and then did an exact `searchTermAbbreviations[term]` lookup. | `repositories` | 35.4 | **41.1**, same hits, alias now firing |

The fixture eval added in `7de5a305` passed throughout. Its cases were written from the same examples that drove the code, so it could only confirm what I had already checked by hand. The new cases — `plural configuration reaches config`, `log a message in json format`, `check in a JSON file`, `sign the request in json format` — are the queries I did not think to write.

Two defects, both mine:

`configurations` scored 10.4 on noise while `configuration` scored 26.5 on the right code. The retrieval loop iterated a pre-morphology snapshot and did an exact table lookup, so no plural ever matched a key. The fixture eval passed through both defects. I wrote its cases from the same examples that drove the code, so it could only ever confirm what I'd already checked by hand. The four cases that catch these bugs are ones I didn't think to write.

message.content: what is phase 0 and what is phase 1?

content.text:
**Phase 0** is investigation, no code. Two questions, maybe ten minutes:

1. **Does the corpus already exist?** `agentic-swebench` runs a "treated" arm that needs each repo checked out at `base_commit` with a prebuilt entire-graph dump. If those checkouts and dumps are already on disk or scripted, the expensive part of a ranking suite is already solved and Phase 1 is just scoring. If not, I need to build checkout-at-base-commit myself.

2. **Does the scoring script already exist?** `search_callee.go` cites "8 of 12 code-gold files were ranked and 0 had the gold hunk verbatim" over eight R30PUB instances. Somebody computed gold-file recall against patches by hand. If that script is in `dev/`, I extend it instead of writing a new one, and I inherit whatever their definition of "ranked" was.

The point of making this a phase rather than just starting is that I have twice now proposed building something that already existed, first the eval generally, then the corpus-scale suite. Checking first is cheap.

**Phase 1** is the smallest thing that produces a real number:

- **Input:** the 30 instances in `agentic-swebench/tasks/pilot_tasks.json`.
- **Query:** `problem_statement`, run through one fixed, documented recipe. I'd report title-only and full-statement as two separate conditions, since full statements carry stack traces and are unlike anything a developer types.
- **Gold:** the files touched by `patch`. File-level only, which needs no oracle and therefore works across all nine languages immediately.
- **Metrics:** recall@1, @5, @10 and MRR.
- **Comparison:** entire-graph `search` against a naive BM25-over-files floor, matching graphmark's house style of always having a floor so the number means something.

Deliberately not: symbol-level gold, editability, the full 300, the held-out split, or the `--check` gate. Those are Phases 2 and 3.

What Phase 1 buys is a first honest number, and more usefully, it will expose whatever I have wrong about query construction before that mistake gets baked into 300 instances and a sealed split. Given the last three things I got wrong were all overgeneralisations from one example, I want the cheapest possible place to be wrong.

Want me to run Phase 0 now?

ceiling both arms' prompts already stated, which agents ignored — runaway sessions ran 8.4 searches,
worst case 23): +2 more resolves, no token change.

## 5. Levers that did NOT work, with numbers, so they are not retried

| lever | result |
|---|---|
| `--top-k` alone (10->20), SHOW left at 10 | +1 instance. Raw recall curve does not survive the wrapper |
| preselection pool 96 -> 256 -> 1024 | recall 76.9% -> 73.1% -> 69.2%. NEGATIVE |
| fixture/snapshot ranking class | +1 instance; did NOT fix the ruff case that motivated it (Rust stayed 33%) |
| unconditional search+grep hybrid | +3.8pt localization for +4% tokens. Rejected on a zero-cost screen |
| search-budget cap 4 -> 2 (config 5) | searches -42%, turns UNCHANGED. Falsified; stopped after 1 run |
| payload budget (TIER curve) | +-2% tokens; TIER 5 and 6 are identical, plateau at 5 |

Ranking levers totalled +7.7pt of gold-file localization and bought resolves, never tokens.

## 6. Product defects found and fixed (independent of the benchmark)

- **`entire graph search` returned ZERO results in every git worktree on `main`.** A linked
  worktree's `.git` is a regular file, so `os.Stat(".git/info/exclude")` returns ENOTDIR (not
  ErrNotExist) and the fatal branch aborted the whole search. Wrappers suppress stderr, so it failed
  silently. Regression test covers the worktree layout, an unresolvable gitdir, an ordinary clone and
  a non-git directory; mutation-checked against the old path.
- `defaultSearchTopK` 10 -> 20, reverting a regression I introduced by conflating breadth with depth
  (the old 20/40 default was expensive because of 40-line snippets, not 20 results).
- New `fixture` file class so snapshot/golden/testdata trees stop outranking source.

## 7. Query wording dominates localization

Search recall for the gold file, disjoint 52-instance set:
- raw issue-text prefix as query: 53.8% @10, 69.2% @20
- distilled one-sentence query: 69.2% @10, 75.0% @20

Query distillation alone recovers 7 of 10 instances where the gold file never appeared in the raw
top-40, 5 of them to rank 1. Measured over 155 live agent calls, agents already distil well (mean 43
chars), so this is not an available lever for the eg arm — but it is the single most important thing
for a human or a badly-written integration to get right.

## 8. Method notes

Seven silent measurement failures were found and fixed during this work, each producing
plausible-looking output while measuring the wrong thing: `prof=()` returning nothing under bash 3.2,
the SHOW=10 cap, `_egsearch.py` stripping payload blocks, a falsification test that could only read
zero, a grading gate that could never fire for the eg arm, reports written to a directory nothing
looked in, and mixed denominators in a subset row. The payload logs, cap markers, gate arithmetic and
run-alignment warnings exist because assuming the harness worked was wrong seven times.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Clone the missing SWE-bench Multilingual repo caches (blob:none partial, full history).
set -uo pipefail
SUITE="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/.." && pwd)"
cd "$SUITE"
MISS=/tmp/ml300_missing_repos.txt
clone_one() {
  local repo="$1" name="$2" dst
  dst="$SUITE/repo-cache/$name"
  if [ -d "$dst/.git" ]; then echo "[skip] $name"; return 0; fi
  rm -rf "$dst.tmp"
  if git clone --quiet --no-checkout --filter=blob:none "https://github.com/$repo.git" "$dst.tmp"; then
    mv "$dst.tmp" "$dst"
    echo "[ok] $repo -> $name ($(du -sh "$dst" | cut -f1))"
  else
    rm -rf "$dst.tmp"
    echo "[FAIL] $repo"
    return 1
  fi
}
export -f clone_one; export SUITE
# 4-way parallel (macOS xargs: no -a, read from stdin)
tr '\t' '\n' < "$MISS" | xargs -P 4 -n 2 bash -c 'clone_one "$0" "$1"'
echo "CLONES DONE"

content.text:
Phase 0 done, and it kills Phase 1 as I designed it. The suite largely exists.

## Q1: does the corpus exist?

Half. `repo-cache/` is gitignored and absent, populated by `tools/ml300_clone.sh` (blob-filtered, no-checkout, 4-way parallel). For our purposes that's **21 distinct repos**, not 300.

But the more important half is committed: **`agentic-swebench/.tune_recall.json` is a materialized 53-instance eval set** carrying `iid`, `repo`, `commit`, `lang`, `gold` (files from the patch) and `ps` (the raw problem statement). Every record has all four. Balanced across nine languages, 5-6 each: C, C++, Go, Java, JavaScript, PHP, Ruby, Rust, TypeScript. The query-and-gold derivation I planned for Phase 1 is already done.

## Q2: does the scoring script exist?

Yes. `tools/recall_agent_query.py` **is** Phase 1, and its design anticipates the things I flagged as risks:

- Three query forms: `title`, `first2`, and `base1` (the baseline agent's own first grep string, recovered from its transcript). That last one is cleverer than anything I proposed.
- `strip_paths()` removes URLs and filenames, because they found the harness-authored query **literally led with the gold file path on 5 of 30 instances**, extracted from the issue's GitHub permalink. They caught their own contamination.
- Gold from `+++ b/` hunks, recall @ top-5, with a stated kill gate of 50%.

Plus `payload_screen.py` + `agg.py` for recall@k on a disjoint set, `query_ab.py`, `fragment_ab.py`, and `freeze_eval_sets.py` for the sealed split.

## What I did not expect

**They already use this as a ranking eval.** `FINDINGS.md` §5 is a table of ranking levers scored by recall, including one that reads exactly like defect 2b territory:

> preselection pool 96 → 256 → 1024 | recall 76.9% → 73.1% → 69.2%. NEGATIVE

Existing baselines: 70% gold recall @5 with paths stripped. On a disjoint 52-instance set, raw issue-text prefix 53.8%@10 / 69.2%@20, distilled one-sentence 69.2%@10 / 75.0%@20.

That last pair is the finding most relevant to us. §7 is titled "Query wording dominates localization," and distillation is worth ~15 points. Our whole PR is about making prose queries survive contact with code vocabulary, and there's already a measured baseline for exactly that axis.

One line I'd want anyone touching this to read first, from §8:

> Seven silent measurement failures were found and fixed during this work, each producing plausible-looking output while measuring the wrong thing.

## Revised plan

Phase 1 is no longer "build it." It's:

1. Clone 21 repos via `ml300_clone.sh` (blob-filtered, so cheap).
2. Point `recall_agent_query.py` at two binaries, `main` and the PR branch, over the 53 committed instances.
3. Report gold-file recall@5 and @10 per query form, per language.

That's a real corpus-scale number for PR #248 today, against 53 human-written queries from people who never saw our alias table. Given Thomas found two bugs my fixture eval sailed past, that's exactly the missing check.

What I originally called Phase 3 (productize into a graphmark suite with version stamping, committed baseline, `--check` gate) becomes the actual build work, and it's now clearly worth doing since the measurement already exists ad hoc and keeps getting recomputed by hand.

The one caveat: `recall_agent_query.py` has hardcoded scratchpad paths from Suhaan's machine for the default binary, and `base1` needs transcripts from prior baseline runs we don't have. So `title` and `first2` will work; `base1` will silently yield nothing. Given §8, I'd verify that rather than trust it.

Want me to run it?

Run the recall harness against #248. Everything else waits on that number.

## 1. Measure the PR properly

Thomas found two bugs my fixture eval passed straight through, because I wrote its cases from the same examples that drove the code. `recall_agent_query.py` over the committed 53-instance set is the fix for that: 53 issue statements written by people who never saw our alias table, across nine languages.

Concretely: clone the 21 repos via `ml300_clone.sh`, run `title` and `first2` query forms against both binaries, report gold-file recall@5 and @10 per language. Existing baseline to beat is 70% @5 with paths stripped.

Two things to handle rather than trust. The script has hardcoded scratchpad paths from Suhaan's machine, and `base1` needs transcripts from prior baseline runs we do not have, so it will silently produce nothing. And given `FINDINGS.md` §8 records seven silent measurement failures in this exact harness, I would sanity-check it first by scoring a deliberately crippled binary and confirming the number drops. A harness that cannot fail is not measuring.

## 2. Then decide on #248

With a corpus number the PR either merges or gets another round. Right now it has unit tests, a fixture tripwire that demonstrably misses things, and a zero-diff negative control from suites that never call `search`. That is thin for a ranking change.

## 3. Defect 2b, now unblocked

It was parked for want of an instrument. The instrument exists. `FINDINGS.md` §5 even has an adjacent measured lever, preselection pool 96 to 1024 dropping recall 76.9% to 69.2%, which is the same neighbourhood as the body-level BM25 question.

## 4. Productize the harness into a graphmark suite

Version stamp, committed baseline, `--check` gate, matching `bench.py`'s conventions. Worth doing precisely because the measurement already exists and keeps being recomputed by hand in scratch scripts with hardcoded paths.

## Smaller, genuinely useful

**Cross-reference graphmark from entire-graph.** Four comments cite R30PUB to justify shipped defaults and none says where the data lives. Took an org-wide code search to find it.

**File the cross-repo provenance issue against the CLI.** Still unfiled, and it is the one finding here with product rather than engineering value: agent work in a sibling repo silently loses commit linkage, and we hit it on Entire's own repos in a session that began with you asking me to trace provenance.

## Loose ends from earlier

The `cli` working tree still has the uncommitted `CLAUDE.md` change and untracked skill files from the first turn. Its 19 checkpoint refs for this session were never pushed. Your `entire` CLI is still 0.9.0 against 0.10.6.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Gold-file recall for N entire-graph binaries over the committed 53-instance set.

Adapted from tools/recall_agent_query.py. Differences, all deliberate:
  - iterates .tune_recall.json (53 instances, 9 languages, gold + problem statement
    already materialized) instead of rep30_tasks.json
  - takes the binary per arm instead of a hardcoded scratchpad path
  - ISOLATES --cache-dir per arm. Sharing it across binaries would let one arm read
    the other's index and silently measure nothing.
  - top-k 10, scoring @5 and @10
  - drops the base1 query form: it needs baseline-arm transcripts we do not have,
    and would silently contribute zero
"""
import json, os, re, subprocess, sys, time

SUITE = os.path.abspath(".")
WTROOT = "/tmp/recall_wt"
ARMS = {"main": "/tmp/graphmark-bin/eg-main", "pr": "/tmp/graphmark-bin/eg-td"}
TOPK = 10

sys.path.insert(0, os.path.join(SUITE, "tools"))
from recall_agent_query import strip_paths  # reuse the leak-stripping verbatim


def queries_for(ps):
    body = strip_paths(ps or "")
    lines = [l.strip() for l in (ps or "").strip().splitlines() if l.strip()]
    title = strip_paths(lines[0]) if lines else ""
    sents = re.split(r"(?<=[.!?])\s+", body)
    q = {}
    if title:
        q["title"] = title[:200]
    if sents:
        q["first2"] = " ".join(sents[:2])[:240]
    return {k: v for k, v in q.items() if v and len(v) > 8}


def ensure_wt(cache, commit, wt):
    src = os.path.join(SUITE, "repo-cache", cache)
    if not os.path.isdir(src):
        return None
    if os.path.isdir(wt):
        return wt
    os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(wt), exist_ok=True)
    r = subprocess.run(["git", "-C", src, "worktree", "add", "--force", "--detach", wt, commit],
                       capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=1800)
    return wt if r.returncode == 0 else None


def run_query(binpath, arm, wt, iid, q):
    cmd = [binpath, "search", "--query", q, "--repo", wt, "--profile", "full",
           "--format", "text", "--top-k", str(TOPK), "--max-snippet-lines", "2",
           "--max-context-bytes", "3000",
           "--cache-dir", os.path.join(SUITE, ".eg_cache_%s" % arm, iid)]
    try:
        r = subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=1800)
    except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
        return None
    paths = []
    for ln in (r.stdout or "").splitlines():
        m = re.match(r"^\s*(\d+)\.\s+(\S+?):", ln)
        if m and m.group(2) not in paths:
            paths.append(m.group(2))
    return paths[:TOPK]


def main():
    tasks = json.load(open(".tune_recall.json"))
    out = open("/tmp/recall_rows.ndjson", "w")
    for n, t in enumerate(tasks, 1):
        iid, gold = t["iid"], set(t["gold"])
        wt = ensure_wt(t["cache"], t["commit"], "%s/%s" % (WTROOT, iid))
        if not wt:
            print("%3d/%d %-34s SKIP no worktree" % (n, len(tasks), iid), flush=True); continue
        qs = queries_for(t.get("ps"))
        rec = {"iid": iid, "lang": t["lang"], "gold": sorted(gold), "arms": {}}
        for arm, binpath in ARMS.items():
            rec["arms"][arm] = {}
            for form, q in qs.items():
                t0 = time.time()
                top = run_query(binpath, arm, wt, iid, q)
                rec["arms"][arm][form] = {
                    "top": top, "secs": round(time.time() - t0, 1),
                    "hit5": bool(top) and any(g in top[:5] for g in gold),
                    "hit10": bool(top) and any(g in top for g in gold),
                    "parsed": 0 if top is None else len(top),
                }
        out.write(json.dumps(rec) + "\n"); out.flush()
        mk = "".join("%s%s" % (a[0].upper(), "Y" if rec["arms"][a].get("title", {}).get("hit10") else "-")
                     for a in ARMS)
        print("%3d/%d %-34s %-11s [%s]" % (n, len(tasks), iid, t["lang"], mk), flush=True)
    out.close()
    print("DONE")


main()
PYEOF

content.text:
Step 1 is done, and it changes step 2. **I do not think #248 should merge as it stands.**

## The number

53 real SWE-bench issue statements, nine languages, gold = files touched by the human fix. Both binaries, isolated caches, JSON output with an unbounded budget.

| form | metric | main | PR |
|---|---|---|---|
| title | recall@5 | 52.8% | **50.9%** |
| title | recall@10 | 66.0% | **64.2%** |
| first2 | recall@5 | 56.6% | 56.6% |
| first2 | recall@10 | 60.4% | 60.4% |
| title | MRR | 0.3925 | **0.3813** |
| first2 | MRR | 0.4253 | **0.4156** |

Every metric is flat or slightly worse. Nothing improved.

## It is not inertness

I checked, because "the feature never fires" would be a different story. The abbreviation table fires on **36%** of these queries and the compound table on 6%. And only **48% of top-10 rankings are identical**, so the PR is moving results on half the corpus. It moves them to a net-negative outcome.

Eleven instances changed rank. Five wins (fmt-3272 went 0.5 to 1.0, laravel 0.5 to 1.0), six losses, losses slightly heavier.

## Two regressions, one diagnosed

**caddy-5870, verified.** Query "return 4xx on invalid input for **delete** method". My table maps `delete → del`. I rebuilt with that single entry removed and the gold file returned to rank 6, exactly matching main. Confirmed cause, not a guess.

That points at a class defect rather than one bad row. The table contains entries where the long form is *also* what code writes: delete/Delete, error/Error, string/String, length/Length, number/Number, max/Max. For those the alias buys nothing and adds noise. The entries that earn their place are the ones where code essentially never spells the long form: authentication, configuration, repository, implementation, specification. The table needs pruning by that rule.

**vuejs core-11899, undiagnosed.** Gold dropped rank 1 to rank 5 on both query forms, the largest single loss. A bisect puts it in my four commits, not Thomas's: main ranks it 1, my pre-Thomas build ranks it 5, current ranks it 5. I have not isolated which of the three mechanisms causes it, and after being wrong three times this session I am not going to guess.

## A bug in the existing harness

`recall_agent_query.py` runs `--format text --max-context-bytes 3000`. At `--top-k 10` that emits **4** ranked paths on the instance I probed; JSON unbounded emits 10. So its published "gold-file recall @ top-5" was really recall over whatever survived the payload budget. That belongs on graphmark's list, and it is precisely the failure mode their own `FINDINGS.md` §8 warns about seven times over.

## Where this leaves things

The improvement evidence is entirely hand measurements on `entireio/cli`, a repo I was staring at while writing the code. On 53 queries written by strangers, the same changes are neutral-to-negative. That is the tension, and I would rather state it than bury it in a merge.

What I would do: prune the alias table to entries where the long form is genuinely rare in code, isolate the vue regression, re-run, and only merge on a corpus number that is at least flat. The compound-joining and token-boundary work may well survive that; the alias table as written does not.

Shall I do the pruning and re-run, or do you want to look at the numbers first?

content.text:
Bisect landed: the vue regression is **commit 3, token-boundary matching**. Commits 1 and 2 rank gold at 1, exactly like main; adding `36b2d8cf` drops it to 5. Both regressions are now diagnosed to a mechanism, so here's how we solve it, structurally rather than by whack-a-mole:

## 1. Replace my hand-curated alias table with a measured criterion

The caddy failure is a class, not a row. `delete → del` is bad because *both* spellings are common in identifiers (`Del()` is all over an HTTP codebase), while `authentication → auth` is good because code essentially never spells the long form. That's a measurable ratio, and we already have the instrument: `entire-graph symbols` NDJSON over the 21 SWE-bench repos plus the 18 fidelity repos gives token frequencies for free.

Rule: keep an entry only where the alias dominates the long form in identifier tokens (say ≥4x) and the alias isn't itself a super-common tiny token. `delete`, `error`, `number`, `max`, `message` fall out; `authentication`, `configuration`, `repository`, `implementation` survive. The table stops being my taste and becomes an artifact with a derivation, which is the only version of it that should merge.

## 2. Decide commit 3's fate on corpus evidence, not sentiment

Token-boundary matching has the weakest case now: its motivating fix (login vs logging) is *already delivered by compound joining*, since the query carries `login` as a term either way, and its measured corpus cost is a rank-1 → 5 loss. The commit even declared "config no longer matches configure" an acceptable cost; vue may be exactly that cost materializing. I won't guess at the term. The honest move is to run the 53-corpus per-arm: `main`, pruned-alias-only, pruned+compound, full. Keep the cut that's flat-or-better. My prior: compound joining and pruned retrieval-aliasing survive, commit 3 gets carved out into its own PR to reland with evidence.

## 3. Guard against overfitting to the 53

We're now tuning on the eval, which is how this session's mistakes happen at corpus scale. Before merge, one validation pass on a fresh hash-selected slice of `multilingual_300` (instances not in the 53). Tune on 53, confirm on held-out, then decide.

## 4. Feed the findings back

- caddy and vue shapes go into the fixture eval as tripwires.
- The harness truncation bug (text/3000 emits 4 of 10 ranks, so graphmark's published recall@5 was really recall@~4) gets filed against graphmark. Their §8 lists seven silent measurement failures; this is the eighth.
- PR #248 and #247 get the corpus verdict either way, per your standing rule.

**Merge gate:** corpus flat-or-better on recall@5/@10 and MRR, held-out slice confirms, cli case studies still pass. The cli wins were real but they were measured on the repo I was staring at; 53 strangers' queries outvote them.

Cost: alias-frequency script plus rebuilds ~30 min, two new arms on the 53 ~70 min, held-out ~30 min.

The quiet win here: this is the first change in this repo's ranking history that gets decided by an instrument instead of a hand-measured anecdote. That was the actual point of the last two days.

Want me to run it? I'd start with the frequency-pruned table, since every downstream decision needs that build.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Identifier-token frequencies for every (long form, alias) pair in the abbreviation table,
measured over a multi-language corpus: one worktree per distinct SWE-bench repo (21, nine
languages), the 18 graphmark fidelity Go repos, and entireio/cli. Decides which table entries
earn their place with a number instead of taste."""
import json, os, re, subprocess, sys, collections

EG = "/tmp/graphmark-bin/eg-td"
SRC = "/Users/krk/Desktop/GitStore/entire-graph/internal/sem/search.go"

# one worktree per distinct swebench repo
tune = json.load(open("/Users/krk/Desktop/GitStore/graphmark/agentic-swebench/.tune_recall.json"))
seen, repos = set(), []
for t in tune:
    if t["cache"] in seen: continue
    seen.add(t["cache"])
    wt = "/tmp/recall_wt/" + t["iid"]
    if os.path.isdir(wt): repos.append((t["cache"], wt))
gm = "/Users/krk/Desktop/GitStore/graphmark/corpus"
for name in sorted(os.listdir(gm)):
    p = os.path.join(gm, name)
    if os.path.isdir(os.path.join(p, ".git")) or os.path.exists(os.path.join(p, ".git")):
        repos.append(("fid_"+name, p))
repos.append(("cli", "/Users/krk/Desktop/GitStore/cli"))
print("corpus repos:", len(repos), file=sys.stderr)

tok_split = re.compile(r"[^A-Za-z0-9]+")
hump = re.compile(r"(?<=[a-z0-9])(?=[A-Z])|(?<=[A-Z])(?=[A-Z][a-z])")
def tokens(name):
    for part in tok_split.split(name):
        for t in hump.split(part):
            if t: yield t.lower()

counts = collections.Counter(); total = 0
for label, wt in repos:
    try:
        r = subprocess.run([EG, "symbols", "--repo", wt, "--format", "ndjson",
                            "--worktree", "--profile", "syntax-only"],
                           capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=1800)
    except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
        print("TIMEOUT", label, file=sys.stderr); continue
    n = 0
    for line in r.stdout.splitlines():
        try: o = json.loads(line)
        except Exception: continue
        nm = o.get("symbol_name") or o.get("name")
        if not nm: continue
        n += 1
        for t in tokens(nm): counts[t] += 1; total += 1
    print("%-28s symbols=%d" % (label, n), file=sys.stderr)

# pull the table out of search.go
src = open(SRC).read()
m = re.search(r"var searchTermAbbreviations = map\[string\]\[\]string\{(.*?)\n\}", src, re.S)
pairs = []
for long_, aliases in re.findall(r'"([^"]+)":\s*\{([^}]*)\}', m.group(1)):
    for a in re.findall(r'"([^"]+)"', aliases):
        pairs.append((long_, a))

out = []
for long_, alias in pairs:
    cl, ca = counts.get(long_, 0), counts.get(alias, 0)
    out.append({"long": long_, "alias": alias, "n_long": cl, "n_alias": ca,
                "per_100k_long": round(1e5*cl/total, 2), "ratio": round(ca/cl, 1) if cl else None})
json.dump({"total_tokens": total, "pairs": out}, open("/tmp/token_freq.json", "w"), indent=1)
print("total identifier tokens: %d, pairs: %d -> /tmp/token_freq.json" % (total, len(pairs)), file=sys.stderr)
PYEOF

fix(search): derive the abbreviation table from identifier frequencies

The hand-written table carried 74 pairs and lost a real query to one of
them: "return 4xx on invalid input for delete method" (SWE-bench
caddyserver__caddy-5870) dropped its gold file out of the top ten,
because delete -> del pulled every Del() header helper into the head.
Verified by removal: deleting that one entry restored the gold file to
rank 6, exactly matching the pre-table build.

The failure class, not the failure row: an entry earns its place only
when the query genuinely needs help. That is false when the long form is
already common in identifiers (code writes "delete" in symbol names 10x
more often than "del") and false when code does not actually prefer the
short form (txn occurs ONCE in 1.4M identifier tokens; sess zero).

Keep rule, measured over 1.4M identifier tokens from 40 repos (21
SWE-bench Multilingual repos across nine languages, 18 pinned Go repos,
entireio/cli): alias outnumbers long form at least 2:1 AND the long form
occurs at most 50 per 100k tokens. Applied mechanically, no hand
exceptions: 43 of 74 pairs pruned, 31 kept. Casualties include
delete/del, context/ctx, error/err, database/db (code prefers the LONG
form 3:1), transaction/txn. Survivors are the prose-word-code-never-
writes class: authentication/auth (125 vs 434), configuration/config
(418 vs 4073), specification/spec (14 vs 3101).

Corpus effect (53 tuning + 30 sealed held-out SWE-bench instances,
gold = files touched by the human fix):
  caddy regression        fixed, gold back at main parity
  recall@10               flat on both sets, both query forms
  recall@5                +1 instance (tuning), -1 instance (held-out)
  MRR                     -0.004 (tuning), -0.015 (held-out)
The residual MRR cost is two rank-1 losses (vuejs__core-11899,
preactjs__preact-2896) attributable to the token-boundary commit, whose
diagnosis is recorded there: the old substring scoring triple-counted
morphological variants of one query word, and those two golds were
winning through the artifact. Across both sets the same commit improves
gold rank on nine other (instance, form) pairs.

All cli case studies hold: "authentication" 36.7 all-auth head, the
headline login query, plural configurations, repositories.

Refs #247.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
MSGEOF
